(c) Infidelity $1-F$ as a function of the effective flux-drive amplitude $A\equiv A_{\varphi}|\varphi_{01}|$ near the optimized operating point, with $A_{n}$ adjusted to preserve the packet-strength matching condition $N_{\varphi}A_{\varphi}|\varphi_{01}|=N_{n}A_{n}|n_{01}|$ . Leakage stays below $10^{-4}$ while infidelity reaches the $10^{-4}$ level over a finite drive range.

fields.result: Unary position encoding compressed into fixed-size circuits of about 200 two-qubit gates resolves double-well tunneling, dropping right-well probability from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM Phoenix and 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ Forte. Binary product formulas require several thousand two-qubit gates and fail to show population transfer.
fields.question: Can real-time bosonic dynamics discretized on a position lattice be simulated faithfully on noisy quantum hardware using binary versus unary encodings?
fields.limits: Post-selected on single-excitation code space. Exact fixed-size circuit compression holds only for single degrees of freedom; inter-register interactions prevent exact compression in coupled-oscillator systems.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12 : Double-well probability dynamics with 14-site unary encoding. Waterfall plots show (a) exact-grid, (b) ideal product-formula, (c) IBM Phoenix, and (d) IonQ Forte results during the first interwell transfer. Snapshots (e–g) and (h–j) show the corresponding IBM Phoenix and IonQ Forte distributions at the initial, intermediate, and transfer times. Colored bars represent measured site probabilities conditioned on single-excitation acceptance, while gray filled and dashed profiles denote exact-grid and ideal product-formula predictions, respectively. Color indicates time, and $P(x>0)$ denotes the right-well probability.
fields.figure_gloss: Position probability distributions versus coordinate $x$ and time $t$ for 14-site unary double-well dynamics. Both IBM Phoenix and IonQ Forte capture the coherent wave-packet tunneling from the right well to the left well, matching exact-grid and ideal product-formula baselines.

fields.result: Ultraviolet-free three-step photoionization scheme achieves 0 detected contaminant ions across all 997 loaded $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ ions, with calculated unwanted-isotope fraction suppressed from $\epsilon_1 = 5.94 \times 10^{-4}$ after the first step down to $\epsilon_2 \simeq 6.8 \times 10^{-7}$.
fields.question: Can high-purity, rapid isotope-selective loading of $^{137}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ or $^{135}\mathrm{Ba}^{+}$ be achieved from a natural-abundance source without using ultraviolet photoionization beams?
fields.limits: Final 532 nm step operates in an unsaturated regime over measured intensity range of 2.2 kW/cm$^2$ to 13.4 kW/cm$^2$. Model selectivity values assume specific Voigt linewidths and thermal atomic beam geometry.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Relayed isotope selectivity. Calculated undesired-isotope excitation fractions after the $791\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ step (upper map, $\epsilon_{1}$ ) and after both resonant steps (lower map, $\epsilon_{2}$ ), using a common logarithmic color scale. The $791\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ laser addresses the ${}^{137}\mathrm{Ba}$ $F^{\prime}=1/2$ line. The circle marks $(\Gamma_{L,791},\Gamma_{G,791})=(8.24,31.4)$ MHz from the model analysis of the measured $791\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ spectrum in Fig. 2 (see Supplemental Material [ 25 ] ). The arrow and frame indicate that the lower map retains the isotope and intermediate-state weights at this circle while varying the second-step widths. The $554\text{\,}\mathrm{n}\mathrm{m}$ laser addresses the ${}^{137}\mathrm{Ba}$ $F^{\prime}=1/2\rightarrow F^{\prime\prime}=1/2$ line. The star marks $(\Gamma_{L,554},\Gamma_{G,554})=(35.2,56.9)$ MHz from the joint fit in Fig. 3 , giving $\epsilon_{2}\simeq 6.8\times 10^{-7}$ . The calculation uses the line positions listed in the Supplemental Material [ 25 ] and common widths for all second-step components.
fields.figure_gloss: Calculated fraction of unwanted isotopes excited after the 791 nm transition alone (upper map) and after sequential resonant transfer at 554 nm (lower map) as functions of the laser Gaussian and Lorentzian linewidths. Relayed selectivity suppresses contaminant fraction by roughly 870-fold under experimental linewidths.

fields.result: Adding one completion qubit per noncommuting check pair yields globally commuting Clifford checks while preserving code distance $d(\widehat{P}_{g})=d(P_{g})$, giving logical measurements with circuit fault distance $\Omega(d)$ in $O(d)$ rounds.
fields.question: Can logical measurements by gauging be implemented via globally commuting checks with bounded fault propagation over repeated measurement rounds?
fields.prior: was noncommuting raw checks that randomize outcomes outside code space and require multi-round tracking (Lavasani 2024)
fields.limits: Restricted to Clifford $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ symmetries on disjoint bounded-size matter blocks; exact commuting completion fails across mixed qubit–qutrit hierarchies for $D(S_3)$.

Each face contains three completion qubits and is indexed by its southwest vertex. (b),(c) The flux $B_{c,f}$ controls the pinning check $T_{c,f}=T(B_{c,f},t_{c,f})$ on face $f$ . (d)–(f) Raw stars $A_{c,u}$ and their completions $\widehat{A}_{c,u}$ for $c=r,g,b$ , with $\Delta=(1,1)$ . fields.result: Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) qubit quantum secure direct communication achieves transmission beyond 1000 km with 23 dB squeezing and 2750 third-generation repeater nodes.
fields.question: Can quantum secure direct communication be extended to long distances by combining Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill qubits with third-generation quantum repeaters?
fields.prior: Experimental demonstrations achieved 100 km in 2022 and 300 km in a 4-user network, both without quantum repeaters.
fields.limits: Simulated under 23 dB squeezing, neglect of phase-space envelopes (low-probability odd/even multiple displacement events omitted), and fiber coupling/homodyne detection efficiency product of $\eta_{0}\eta_{h}=0.98$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Performance analysis as a function of total communication distance for $N$ = 500 with coupling and measurement efficiencies $\eta_{0}\eta_{h}$ = 0.98, and squeezing level of 23 dB. (a) the optimal number of repeater nodes, (b) the minimum cost function, (c) the secrecy message capacity with optimal repeater configuration, and (d) corresponding repeater spacing under different transmission distance.
fields.figure_gloss: Repeater performance plotted versus total communication distance up to 300 km under an upper bound of $N=500$ nodes, showing optimal node count, minimized resource cost, secrecy message capacity, and optimal repeater spacing.

fields.result: GQE transformer policy trained directly on a 70-qubit processor generates state-preparation circuits that recover energies within 15 mHa of DMRG across 27 of 28 test runs (median 4.5 mHa). Circuits at 56–70 qubits require 34–72 times fewer two-qubit gates than transpiled LUCJ ansätze.
fields.question: Can generative quantum eigensolver policies be trained directly with quantum hardware feedback at active spaces up to 70 qubits beyond exact classical simulation?
fields.limits: Single training run per lineage. Evaluated on 10 sampled circuits per molecule with up to 100,000 shots per circuit; subspace recovery capped at 20,000 strings.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Raw-shot excitation composition (HF, S, D, T, Q, higher; percent of 100,000 shots) of the ten circuits sampled by the A1 policy trained at 46 qubits with the Hartree–Fock penalty, for each of the eleven compounds, ordered from the smallest to the largest active space. Numbers above each column are the circuit depth as-submitted to ibm_kobe ; “best” and “2nd” mark the two circuits with the lowest ranking energy, and “E+D 1st” and “E+D 2nd” the two circuits chosen by the combined energy and distinct-bitstring rank (a circuit can carry two labels). In every compound the best circuit puts at most 1.2% of its shots in “higher” and is among the four shallowest of the ten (the shallowest in four of the eleven panels); the second circuit does so in eight of the eleven panels, and in the SnOH3-me L, SnOH3-me-h2o M and SnOH3-me-2h2o M panels it has essentially all its weight in “higher”. Most of the other circuits are one to three orders of magnitude deeper with all their weight in “higher”.
fields.figure_gloss: Excitation distribution (HF, single, double, triple, quadruple, higher) plotted across 10 sampled circuits for eleven organotin molecules from 32 to 70 qubits, showing physical shot spread across excitation manifolds without collapsing to Hartree–Fock.

fields.result: Online contextual-bandit selection across five mitigation arms achieves 95.5% of omniscient oracle utility across 80 conditions, outperforming all six static policies (Friedman $\chi^2=92.18$, $p\approx1.1\times10^{-17}$). On snapshots from eight IBM devices, it reaches 99.9% of oracle utility at a constant budget of roughly $1.3\times10^4$ shots for three to eight qubits.
fields.question: Can an online controller that observes only standard variational feedback signals select error mitigation techniques dynamically to outperform any single static mitigation policy across different quantum machine learning paradigms?
fields.limits: Evaluated on a fixed cost-aware utility function balancing quality against shot overhead. Real-device tests limited to simulated noise from 8 calibration snapshots across 32 blocks. Mitigation techniques are treated as mutually exclusive rather than composable.
tools: error mitigation pool (ZNE, PEC, MEM, DD, circuit optimization)
IBM Quantum hardware noise calibration snapshots
variational quantum algorithms (VQC, QSVM, VQE, generative models, QRL)

fields.result: Real rational functions $R(x)$ bounded by $[0,1]$ with no poles on $[-1,1]$ can be synthesized exactly on quantum walks with controller memory dimension $d$ satisfying rational degree $r \le d^2$, bypassing polynomial approximation.
fields.question: Can a finite-memory repeat-until-success architecture with mid-circuit measurements implement rational spectral effects exactly without polynomial approximation?
fields.limits: Requires uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry; spectrum of Hermitian operator $X$ must lie in $[-1,1]$; bounds derived under fresh-copy, terminal-postselection restarting model.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Rational quantum spectral filtering by RUS. (a) Protocol architecture. A controlled-walk router $\Gamma_{W}$ and a fixed unitary colligation $\mathsf{U}$ act on the signal, controller memory, and measurement flag. Each round produces one of three outcomes. (b) First-hitting representation of the protocol. The continuation operator $C$ generates successive controller states, while terminal operators $\mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{a}}$ and $\mathsf{T}_{\mathsf{r}}$ describe acceptance and rejection after an arbitrary number of iterations. (c) Rational spectral response. Summation over all first-hitting histories produces a rational acceptance probability $R(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ , which reweights the input spectral distribution and enables selective spectral filtering.
fields.figure_gloss: RUS protocol framework showing the circuit architecture, first-hitting transition graph, and resulting rational spectral filtering response $R(x)=P(x)/Q(x)$ across eigenvalue $x$.

fields.result: A $5\times 5$ persymmetric Jacobi matrix with centered spectrum $\{c-x,c-y,c,c+y,c+x\}$ realizing perfect state transfer lacks early state exclusion if and only if $x$ is an integer multiple of $y$. Any prescribed even number $2k$ of early state exclusions can be generated by setting positive eigenvalues $y=2k+1$ and $x=2k+2$.
fields.question: Can early state exclusion occur in a 1D quantum spin chain of 5 qubits that realizes perfect state transfer?
fields.prior: Early state exclusion was proven impossible for 3 qubits and constructed for all even numbers of qubits, but remained open for all odd numbers $n>4$.
fields.limits: Applies strictly to $5\times 5$ Jacobi matrices with centered or symmetric spectra and nearest-neighbor interactions; odd qubit counts $n\ge 7$ remain unproven.

fields.result: Classical fidelity of continuous normalizing flows over $(S^{2})^{N}$ phase space reaches $F \approx 0.96$ at $N=64$ qubits for 1D cluster states and $0.985$ at gate 40 for a 10-qubit TFIM VQE circuit.
fields.question: Can quantum circuits be simulated classically by parameterizing unitary gates as normalizing flows between phase-space probability distributions on $(S^2)^N$?
fields.prior: For 1D cluster states at $N=60$, IC-POVM reached $0.91$ and NQS reached $0.84$; for 10-qubit TFIM VQE, transformer IC-POVM reached $0.965$.
fields.limits: Training cost scales as $\mathcal{O}(K^{2})$ for $K$ gates because evaluating prior states requires inverting all previous flows; entangling-gate flows are state-dependent and cannot be reused for different input states.

fields.result: Formulated noninterference $\mathsf{NI}$ and simulation-based $\mathsf{SIM}$ security for quantum programs, proved $\mathsf{NI} \Leftrightarrow \mathsf{SIM} \Leftrightarrow \mathsf{SIMQ}$, and developed self-conjugation to verify them via quantum Hoare logic.
fields.question: How do we formally define and verify information-flow security for quantum programs?
fields.limits: Loop-free quantum programs with finite-dimensional variable types (or fixed-bound unrolled loops).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9 . Intuition for self-conjugation in the simple case where $P$ is a circuit $Q$ . Here, program $\mathit{Test}$ is visualized, with $\overline{h}=\mathit{Hvar}(Q)$ and $\overline{l}=\mathit{Lvar}(Q)$ . The red flow indicates confidential information. The LHS illustrates an insecure $Q$ , where confidential information stored in $\overline{h}$ leaks to $\overline{l}$ and is swapped to $\overline{l^{\prime}}$ , so $\mathit{rev}(Q)$ cannot fully recover the original state of $\overline{h}$ . The RHS illustrates a secure $Q$ , where $\mathit{rev}(Q)$ can fully recover the confidential information because it has not leaked.
fields.figure_gloss: Information flow through circuit $Q$ and its reverse $Q^{\dagger}$. Red lines mark secret data propagation, comparing insecure flow that leaks into low variables against secure flow confined to high and environmental variables.

fields.result: Trimerized valence-bond solid phase extends to $\alpha_{c2} \gtrsim 3.5$ and terminates below $\alpha \approx 5$, ruling out lower boundary around $\alpha \approx 2$. Large-$\alpha$ effective central charge is consistent with massless flow from $\mathrm{SU(3)}_2$ to $\mathrm{SU(3)}_1$.
fields.question: Where does the trimerized phase terminate in the frustrated $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ Heisenberg chain as a function of $\alpha = J_2/J_1$?
fields.prior: Estimates for upper boundary ranged from $\alpha \approx 2.1$ via exact diagonalization to $\alpha \approx 3.8$ via iDMRG.
fields.limits: 1D chain at zero temperature; virtual bond dimension up to $D \approx 8000$.

fields.result: Simulated nonperturbative flux-string dynamics in a $(2+1)\text{D}$ $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and plaquette terms for up to 15 Trotter steps ($t = 4.5$ in units of $J_{v}$). Spatially resolved measurements show rapid charge and flux spreading in deconfined regimes, matter creation inside the string near resonance ($h_{z}/J_{v} = 2.00$), and suppressed spreading at large electric fields ($h_{z}/J_{v} = 4.00$).
fields.question: Can quantum processors simulate the real-time, nonperturbative dynamics and transverse fluctuations of electric flux strings in a $(2+1)\text{D}$ lattice gauge theory while exploiting gauge redundancy for error detection?
fields.limits: Restricted to diagonal local observables and string-like projectors via marginal distributions to manage exponential post-selection sampling overhead; limited to total evolution time $t=4.5$ ($dt=0.3$).

( B ) Measured string projector $\langle\prod_{k\in\gamma}n_{k}\rangle$ on the links of each string $\gamma$ , for the initial string (left), summed over the two strings 1 plaquette (center) and 2 plaquettes (right) away, for the four values of $h_{z}$ .

fields.result: Phase-matching in a homogeneous 912-SNAIL JTWPA achieved without integrated resonators by exploiting coil field inhomogeneity and flux focusing, producing broadband 3-wave mixing gain across $4\text{ GHz}-8\text{ GHz}$ for $\Phi \gtrsim 6\Phi_{0}$ with a 12 GHz pump.
fields.question: Can an inhomogeneous external magnetic field provide phase-matching in a uniform Josephson traveling wave parametric amplifier without on-chip resonant structures?
fields.limits: Measurements conducted at $15\text{ mK}$; requires sufficiently large magnetic flux offsets $\Phi \gg \Phi_{0}$; gain onset is sensitive to the spatial profile of the magnetic field distribution along the meandered array.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) Experimental normalized transmission measurements through the JTWPA as a function of the signal frequency and external magnetic flux for pump frequencies of $101112\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$ at pump powers $P_{\mathrm{p}}=$-71-72-74\text{\,}\mathrm{dBm}$$ , correspondingly. At low values of the external magnetic flux $\Phi\sim\Phi_{0}$ , the 4WM process is efficient due to a limited phase-matching. At larger values of $\Phi\gg\Phi_{0}$ , the 3WM process becomes phase-matched, which leads to a broadband amplification response, characterized by a bandwidth $\sim$4\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$$ . We mark corresponding threshold values of magnetic flux with double arrows labeled $\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}(f)$ . (b) Three-mode theoretical model of the JTWPA response in an inhomogeneous magnetic field at pump frequencies of $101112\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$ at a fixed pump power of $P_{\mathrm{p}}=$-74\text{\,}\mathrm{dBm}$$ (see Appendix B for more details). (c) Multi-mode harmonic-balance simulations of the JTWPA response in an inhomogeneous magnetic field for pump frequencies of $101112\text{\,}\mathrm{GHz}$ at a fixed pump power of $P_{\mathrm{p}}=$-74\text{\,}\mathrm{dBm}$$ . Including additional mode mixing reveals higher-order effects beyond the three-mode approximation (see Appendix C for further details). The three-mode model evaluates the 3WM and 4WM gain separately and keeps the larger of the two at each probe frequency, whereas the multi-mode model solves both simultaneously and retains the additional mixing products.
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized transmission gain as a function of signal frequency and external flux $\Phi$ for pump frequencies of 10, 11, and 12 GHz, showing experimental measurements alongside three-mode and multi-mode simulations that capture the pump-frequency-dependent flux threshold $\Phi_{\mathrm{t}}$ for broadband gain emergence.

fields.result: Disorder-induced soft modes (diffusons) in shared conductors impose dephasing correlations scaling as $\eta_{ij} \approx -\cos(\phi_{i}+\phi_{j})/n^{2}$. Worst-case integrated correlated noise per qubit grows as $2\ln\min(N,Dt/L_{q}^{2})$, violating the standard fault-tolerance threshold condition in two dimensions.
fields.question: What is the spatial structure and array-size scaling of dephasing noise mediated between solid-state qubits by low-energy collective modes in a shared disordered conductor?
fields.limits: Truncated at Gaussian order in charge-density fluctuations. Evaluates disorder-averaged kernel without sample-specific mesoscopic fluctuations or weak-localization corrections from Cooperons. Worst-case scaling assumes absolute value sum without dynamical phase cancellation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: The top two panels (a) show the summed pair correlations $\mathcal{S}$ of three co-aligned qubits with dipole angles $\phi=0^{\circ}$ and $\phi=60^{\circ}$ , in a triangular configuration, ranging from correlated (red) to anti-correlated (blue). fields.result: Double-quantum driving of $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ ensembles in hBN enhances optical readout contrast and yields a 2.6-fold signal-to-noise improvement in AC magnetometry over single-quantum protocols.
fields.question: Can simultaneous driving of both ground-state transitions enable coherent control of the $\Delta m_s = 2$ manifold and improve magnetic sensing in $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ ensembles?

fields.result: Constraining analog QAOA cost duration to $\gamma_{k}\leq 1\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ on 3D Rydberg arrays yields an annealing branch reaching approximation ratio $R_{a}=0.959$ at $p=20$, outperforming single-rounding Goemans-Williamson ($R_{a}=0.948$). Combining this cold-start annealing branch with a GNN warm start yields a portfolio reaching $R_{a}=0.966$.
fields.question: Can an analog QAOA implemented on a three-dimensional Rydberg atom array solve the weighted MaxCut problem by encoding edge weights directly in interatomic couplings without gadgets?
fields.prior: Without the duration constraint, layer-wise optimization of the analog sequence traps in a non-adiabatic basin saturating near $R_{a}\approx 0.77$. The single-rounding Goemans-Williamson classical algorithm achieves $R_{a}=0.948$ on these graphs.
fields.limits: Numerical emulation of 20 randomly weighted 3-regular graphs with 12 vertices. Under Aquila realistic processor noise ($\lambda=1$), optimal depth drops to $p=3$–$5$, performance falls below Goemans-Williamson ($R_{a}=0.826$), and optimal cut probability per shot is 16%.

fields.question: Can higher-harmonic Josephson elements be organized into superconducting loops to create hardware-protected qudits against charge, flux, and quasiparticle noise?

fields.result: Gate-induced shear strain $\varepsilon_{xy}$ pairs with a long-wavelength wave vector $2k_1$ (feature size $\lambda_1 \approx 1.60$ nm) to activate deterministic valley splitting in narrow Si quantum wells, removing the need for ultrasharp interfaces.

fields.prior: Conventional valley splitting requires sharp heterostructure interfaces of characteristic size $\lambda_0 \approx 0.33$ nm providing wave vector $2k_0$.
fields.limits: Simulated device geometry based on tall tungsten via gates; requires shear strain aligned with the [110] or $[1\bar{1}0]$ crystallographic axes.

fields.limits: Five gatemons measured across three chips. Relaxation times are likely limited by spontaneous emission into a 50 $\Omega$ environment via gate coupling capacitance ($C_{c}=1.5\text{ fF}$, $C_{q}=95\text{ fF}$).

fields.result: Under certified and measured cost models across four Hamiltonian families up to 20 qubits, classical simulation remains at least 3.6 orders of magnitude faster than projected fault-tolerant quantum simulation, showing no quantum crossover within tested sizes.
fields.question: Where does practical quantum advantage begin in quantum dynamics simulation when classical baselines and fault-tolerant quantum compilation are continually updated?
fields.prior: Sun et al. (2024) projected fault-tolerant crossover resource estimates for a mixed-field Ising chain; the arena lowered certified quantum runtime 21-fold to 185-fold and cut $T$-gate counts per Trotter step up to fourfold via Hamming-weight phasing.
fields.limits: Quantum hardware not run; all quantum costs projected using surface-code error models ($p=10^{-3}$ to $10^{-4}$). Tested up to 20 qubits; step counts at tight tolerances conditionally extrapolated from looser targets.
tools: multi-agent LLM framework (Claude Opus, OpenAI Codex)

fields.result: Partitioning Pauli strings with an $\mathbb{F}_2$-linear hash restricts exchanges under any $k$-qubit channel to at most $4^k$ predetermined partitions, enabling local deduplication and weak-scaling efficiencies of $68\text{--}74\%$ across $32$ compute nodes with up to $1.6\times 10^{11}$ Pauli strings.

fields.limits: Trotterized dynamics simulations; load balance degrades when tailoring node hashes to avoid communication across many workers ($P \gg 1$).

fields.result: Packing an entire parameter-shift stencil into a single cloud execution job matches SPSA's final 50-job training loss within 4 to 20 jobs on IBM's ibm_fez, reducing metered processor time by 1.6 to 9 times.
fields.question: How should a classical optimizer group independent circuit evaluations into single cloud jobs to reach a target loss in the fewest round trips?
fields.prior: Simultaneous-perturbation stochastic approximation (SPSA) evaluated across matched job and shot budgets, with SPSA reaching target training loss after 35 to 41 jobs.
fields.limits: Evaluated on small circuits ($n \leq 8$, $P \leq 48$ angles, at most 14 CZ gates) using job-mode queue access on a single processor; test accuracy advantage was statistically significant only at $n=8$.

fields.result: Process-isolated orchestration achieves eight-GPU end-to-end speedups of $5.68\times$ (MI300X) and $6.23\times$ (MI355X) on one-gross ($[[144,12,12]]$) circuits, and $6.92\times$ and $7.01\times$ on two-gross ($[[288,12,18]]$) circuits. fields.prior: Original Pêlagos used a single host Python process managing multiple HIP device contexts with serial preprocessing; the new design improves eight-GPU throughput over this baseline by $>2\times$ on one-gross, and by $1.48\times$ (MI300X) and $1.36\times$ (MI355X) on two-gross.

fields.result: ObfusQate composite and delayed gates retain mean compiled normGED of only 0.21 and 0.23, leaving output readable; Q-MaskCut achieves mean normGED of 0.88 and mean output TVD without key of 0.94, dropping to 0.42 normGED after recompilation by provider.

fields.prior: Prior methods (ObfusQate, ECQCO) evaluated on written circuits before compiler optimization; ObfusQate inverse gates maintain normGED 0.94 to 1.00 after compilation only by lengthening execution time 7 to 112 times.

fields.result: Review synthesizes analytical, numerical, and machine-learning quantum control methodologies, detailing error mitigation strategies across detuning, amplitude imprecision, crosstalk, and leakage in closed and open systems.
fields.question: How can quantum system dynamics be steered with high fidelity toward target states or gates despite pulse imprecisions, leakage, and crosstalk?
fields.limits: Focuses on open-loop and closed-loop final-time measurement feedback; excludes real-time continuous feedback and analytical Pontryagin maximum principle derivations.

fields.result: In a two-segment second-generation repeater link, the $[[5,1,3]]$ code achieves higher end-to-end Bell-state fidelity under low incoherent noise (depolarizing and dephasing), whereas the $[[7,1,3]]$ Steane code outperforms it under coherent over-rotation errors. At high noise regimes, direct transmission without coding outperforms both.
fields.question: How do minimal single-error-correcting stabilizer codes behave under realistic circuit-level incoherent and coherent gate noise in a second-generation quantum repeater link?
fields.limits: Simulated two-segment equal-length repeater link; restricted to distance-3 $[[5,1,3]]$ and $[[7,1,3]]$ codes without circuit-level gate optimization; results lack analytical proof and cannot be directly generalized to larger code families.
tools: Depolarizing, dephasing, and over-rotation noise models

fields.result: Closes a deterministic logical $T$ gate on a 2D color-code register via a persistent 3D mediator, maintaining merged spatial code distance $d_M = d$ and showing finite-distance error scaling close to matched 3D memory benchmarks.
fields.question: Can a 3D color-code block stay encoded and protected while mediating consecutive logical $T$ gates on a distinct 2D register without destructive mediator readout?
fields.prior: Consumptive cross-dimensional lattice-surgery schemes (e.g. generalized lattice surgery) destroy the 3D auxiliary state upon logical readout, requiring fresh preparation every gate.
fields.limits: Circuit-level simulations evaluate a Clifford surrogate rather than the noisy non-Clifford $T$ channel; hook-error fault tolerance relies on single-check flag gadgets rather than a global spacetime circuit-level proof.

fields.question: How can logical error correction information be made available to neutral-atom processors as soon as the required measurements are acquired, without waiting for full camera-frame readout?
fields.prior: was a 32-byte packet transfer at microsecond timescales in the initial NVQLink latency demonstration

fields.result: Enhancing measurement strength $\beta_R=O(\log d)$ on only $O(d\log d)$ checks near selected logical supports restores approximate quantum error correction for toric codes at finite bulk strength, while representative equivalence requires 3D deconfinement via enhanced tubes to make Wilson overlap $w\to 1$.
fields.question: Can approximate quantum error correction recoverability and equivalence of separated logical representatives be restored by selectively enhancing measurement accuracy near logical supports while the bulk remains at finite measurement strength?
fields.limits: Conditioned on the all-plus measurement record, fixed logical register size, sufficiently weak local-stochastic noise, and straight logical representatives.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Logical structure of the results. (a) Local errors reveal selected logical information in general CSS encodings. Along toric representatives, accumulated leakage makes logarithmic measurement strength necessary. (b) Strengthening nearby checks restores AQEC at low noise and sufficient width. (c) Once both encodings are recoverable, their representative equivalence still depends on the bulk: the Wilson overlap vanishes in 2D with macroscopic unenhanced fillings, whereas sufficiently enhanced tubes restore it to one in the strict 3D deconfined phase.
fields.figure_gloss: Three core stages: local logical leakage along toric supports demanding logarithmic strength, recovery restoration by selectively enhancing nearby checks, and dimensional contrast in representative equivalence (vanishing in 2D, restored to unity in 3D).

fields.result: Variance-guided measurement group construction (VGMC) reduces energy estimator variance by 18.19%–23.38% relative to optimized initial designs across molecular benchmarks where additional bases are introduced.

fields.prior: Iterative coefficient splitting (ICS) and ad-hoc repacking on fixed groups.

fields.result: Introduces QuantumInputOutput.jl, an open-source Julia framework automating symbolic derivation and numerical simulation of cascaded SLH input-output networks driven by propagating temporal quantum pulse modes via virtual cavities.
fields.question: How can the derivation of effective Hamiltonians and Lindblad operators for open quantum systems driven by propagating temporal pulse modes across multi-component networks be automated?
fields.limits: Restricted to systems where propagating field is concentrated in a small number of discrete temporal modes; less efficient for broad multimode continua or strong temporal entanglement.

The symbolic operators are defined to build an SLH network before translating them to numeric operators or deriving higher-order mean-field equations. The resulting Hamiltonian and Lindblad operators are then used to simulate the dynamics and determine the output modes. Finally, the full dynamics with output cavities are solved. The translation can be avoided by directly defining the numeric operators.

fields.result: Demonstrates statistical quantum phase estimation on an analog simulator without auxiliary qubits, extracting absolute ground-state energies and energy gaps in one- and two-dimensional arrays of up to $N=19$ Rydberg atoms.
fields.question: Can quantum phase estimation and complex-valued Loschmidt echoes be realized on an analog quantum simulator without controlled time evolution or ancilla registers?
fields.limits: Operates within the nearest-neighbor Rydberg blockade approximation ($V_{\rm nn}\gg \Omega, |\Delta|$); systematic phase error is $\mathcal{O}(\tau^2)$ after analytical initial-time bias subtraction, requiring nonzero echo amplitude.
tools: Loschmidt echo phase reconstruction via Cauchy-Riemann relation

fields.result: Presents a four-model pedagogical taxonomy connecting classical Maxwell solvers (mode profiles, Green functions, scattering matrices) to open-system quantum dynamics and photodetection observables across atomic clocks, Rydberg receivers, and cavity QED.
fields.question: When do classical electromagnetic descriptions suffice, and when must quantum states of field or matter be retained explicitly in electromagnetic design?
fields.limits: Treats primarily few-level atomic systems, single/few cavity modes, and linear media under Markovian dissipation models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Four descriptions of field and matter, classified by the information retained in the calculation. Different questions about the same device may call for different combinations.

fields.result: The stabilizer Rényi entropy (SRE) of Dicke states is extensive at all fillings $f=n/L \in (0,1)$ except $f=1/2$, following $M_2(|D_n^L\rangle) = L\,\alpha(f) + 2\log_2 L + c(f) + o(1)$. Average distillable CCZ yield per qubit is non-zero and extensive across all $0 < f < 1$, equalling $\frac{1}{2}f(1-f)[(1-f)^4 + f^4]$ despite $M_2$ scaling only as $2\log_2(\pi L/8) - 1$ at $f=1/2$.
fields.question: How does the non-stabilizerness (magic) of Dicke states scale in the thermodynamic limit at fixed filling, and what is their resource yield for fault-tolerant quantum computing?
fields.prior: SRE was known only for fixed small excitation count $n$ ($M_2 \sim 2n\log_2 L$) or at half-filling where $M_2 \simeq 2\log_2(\pi L/8) - 1$ (large-$L$ approximation by Oliviero et al. 2022).
fields.limits: Asymptotic thermodynamic limit $L \to \infty$ with fixed filling fraction $f = n/L$. Yields fluctuate by $O(L)$ run-to-run (non-self-averaging) due to an emergent hidden phase.
tools: Magnetization projection of tilted-spin product states
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Magic and CCZ yield of Dicke states. (a) SRE per qubit, $M_{2}(D^{L}_{n})/L$ . The dots show the numerically computed exact values for all $n\leq L/2$ at $L=40$ (blue) and $L=400$ (orange), and the crosses show the largest computed size ( $L=7168$ to $8192$ ) at 15 rational fillings. The black line is the closed-form magic density $\alpha(f)$ of Eq. 14 . At a fixed filling $f=n/L$ , the difference between the exact data and $\alpha(f)$ equals $[2\log_{2}L+c(f)+o(1)]/L$ (Eq. 13 ). The dashed line indicates the magic of a $T$ state. The red dash-dotted curve is a lower bound for the magic density of Haar-random states at the same filling [ 29 ] . (b) CCZ yield per qubit using the heralded eight-qubit procedure $\Lambda_{8}$ of Ref. [ 54 ] , applied to blocks of eight qubits. The blue curve is the average rate $g(f)/12=\frac{1}{2}f(1-f)[(1-f)^{4}+f^{4}]$ , and the orange curve is the guaranteed rate $\frac{1}{2}f(1-f)(1-2f)^{2}$ (see Sec. III.3 ). In both panels, the vertical line denotes the filling $f_{*}$ where the magic density is maximal. All results are symmetric under $f\to 1-f$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Magic density per qubit and CCZ yield per qubit plotted versus excitation filling fraction $f$. It shows that SRE vanishes only at $f=1/2$ and the poles, whereas average CCZ extraction rate remains strictly positive across all non-trivial fillings.

fields.result: Agentic evolutionary program synthesis automatically finds fault-tolerant dynamic Clifford circuits for logical state preparation, logical gates, code switching, and code growth, verified by exhaustive fault evaluation.
fields.question: Can automated LLM-driven program evolution discover fault-tolerant quantum circuits across the full stack of logical operations?
fields.prior: Automated discovery via satisfiability solving or RL was limited to distance-five codes, restricted to state preparation, and required orders of magnitude more circuit simulations.
fields.limits: Restricted to stabilizer/Clifford circuits and single-fault verification models ($t=1$ in reported traces).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2 : Overview of the agentic FunSearch method applied to quantum circuits. Left: the prompt, illustrated for a logical CNOT ( $\overline{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ ) between two logical qubits encoded by the $[[5,1,3]]$ perfect code (see Sec. III.2 ). It starts with a natural-language description of the task, followed by a list of the target stabilizers, here the Choi state generators on all physical and reference qubits. These include the code stabilizers, labeled “checks”, and the stabilizers of the Bell pair between the logical and the reference qubits after applying the desired logical operation (here, $\overline{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ ), labeled “after $\overline{\mathrm{CNOT}}$ ”. Additionally, the prompt also specifies the qubit layout, including the locations of the data and ancilla qubits, the allowed couplings for two-qubit gates, the gate set, and a primer on the relevant physics and the fault tolerance requirement. Right: the hybrid agentic FunSearch loop. The LLM writes a Python program defining a circuit following our custom API. The verifier checks if the circuit achieves the target, and obtains the fault tolerance metrics. These metrics, along with the packed (maximizing parallel qubit utilization) circuit, are attached to each program as feedback. The program is then added to the island database, and ranked by these metrics (see Eq. ( 2 )). The best programs from the islands, along with their feedback, are included in the prompt to the LLM in the subsequent generation. In each generation, we instruct the LLM to write scratchpad notes, which serve as memory and are appended to the next generation’s prompt. The best programs from each island migrate to the neighbouring islands periodically. The LLM also calls the verifier directly through tool calls, which lets it test its proposals before submitting its program in each generation. After some generations, we select the best program as the solution.
fields.figure_gloss: The agentic evolutionary program synthesis workflow. Left: prompt specification with targets, layout, and fault-tolerance constraints. Right: LLM tool use, verifier evaluation, island-based database scoring, and inter-generation memory.

fields.result: Non-global entropic recovery map yields entanglement fidelity $F_{\text{Ent}} = 1 - 1.25 t^2 + O(t^3)$ and worst-case fidelity $F_{\min}^2 = 1 - 1.25 t^2 + O(t^3)$ for independent amplitude damping, computed using only $2 \times 2$ unitaries.
fields.question: Can quantum conditional mutual information guide the construction of an explicit, non-global, computationally inexpensive quantum error correction recovery map for independent and correlated amplitude damping noise?
fields.prior: For independent errors, Petz-map recovery achieved $F_{\text{Ent}} = 1 - 1.25 \gamma^2 + O(\gamma^3)$ and $F_{\min}^2 = 1 - 1.15 \gamma^2 + O(\gamma^3)$ (Biswas & Mandayam 2021).
fields.limits: Short codeword length ($n=4$), damping parameter $t \ll 1$ (perturbation expansion up to $O(t^2)$), speed of light assumed $c=\infty$ in the field model.

fields.result: Encodes and decodes up to 1568 real classical values across entire quantum processors without SWAP gates or ancilla qubits by 2-colouring bipartite coupling graphs into shared address and data qubits.
fields.question: How can classical data be parallel-encoded across a quantum processor without SWAP routing overhead or ancilla qubits under limited hardware connectivity?
fields.prior: QPIXL and QCrank required star connectivity between all address and data registers, forcing SWAP routing on planar hardware.
fields.limits: Requires bipartite coupling subgraphs; error rate grows with local qubit degree and state density, requiring 8192–32768 readout shots per basis.

fields.result: Local commuting reflection gluings in the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ plaquette model form a family indexed by units $u \in \mathbb{Z}_N^\times$. Gluings exist for all $N$ at even seam length $L_x$, and at odd $L_x$ if and only if $-1$ is a quadratic residue modulo $N$.
fields.question: Which local reflection gluings of the $\mathbb{Z}_N$ plaquette model on a Klein bottle yield commuting check algebras, and what spectrum results from the obstructed literal seam?
fields.limits: Restricted to local monomial far-corner gluings of the standard bulk plaquette model. No non-stabilizer resources generated within static Clifford/Weyl operations $\mathcal{O}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: (a) Mirror Klein bottle of the site register ( $L_{x}=6$ , $L_{y}=3$ , $a=0$ ; colours A/B). The virtual row $L_{y}$ is row 0 read at column $a-x$ (top labels). A seam plaquette $S_{x}$ keeps $X$ , $Z$ on its near corners; its far corners land on row 0 at columns $j=a-x-1$ and $j+1$ , where the $u$ -family places $Z^{-u_{j}}$ and $X^{1/u_{j+1}}$ (Theorem 1 ). (b) Non-commutation graph of the literal gluing ( $a=0$ ): $S_{x}$ (squares) and $R_{j}$ (circles), labelled by column; $S_{x}$ meets $R_{a-x-2}$ with phase $\omega$ and $R_{a-x}$ with $\omega^{-1}$ , giving two rings of length $L_{x}$ (even $L_{x}$ ) or one of length $2L_{x}$ (odd $L_{x}$ ) (Theorem 3 ). For $N=2$ these are the graphs of Ref. [ 1 ] , Fig. 2(a,b).
fields.figure_gloss: Lattice layout of the mirror Klein bottle in the site register showing the identification of virtual row $L_y$ with row 0 and far-corner placements of seam plaquettes.

fields.result: Any transformation with classical control of computational order on $N$ independent quantum channels can be deterministically, exactly, and universally simulated by fixed-order quantum circuits using at most $N^2$ queries, or catalytically without consuming $N^2-N$ extra queries.
fields.question: Can quantum circuits with classical or quantum control of causal order be simulated efficiently by standard fixed-order quantum circuits?
fields.limits: Simulation for quantum control of order is restricted to unitary channels; classical control simulation applies to independent channels, extended bipartite channels, and quantum instruments.

fields.result: Introduced percolating entanglement quality (PEQ) to benchmark chip-wide graph states across different coupling topologies. Demonstrated on a 64-qubit square-lattice chip with defects, yielding a 52-qubit entanglement cluster and $\mathrm{PEQ}=0.42$.
fields.question: How can chip-wide quantum processor entanglement be benchmarked on a common scale without ignoring individual coupling qualities or coupling topology differences?
fields.prior: Cluster size and entanglement yield (EY) only count connected qubits; chips with full chip-spanning clusters ($\mathrm{EY}=1.00$) show identical size scores despite widely differing link qualities.
fields.limits: Characterizes the prepared graph state rather than general circuit depth or gate fidelities; requires defining or numerically computing the infinite-lattice bond-percolation threshold for the processor topology.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Entanglement map of the 64-qubit square-lattice processor [ 15 ] . (a) Measured negativities $\mathcal{N}$ , with gray dotted links for defect couplings without negativity data. (b) Negativities in descending order, with one-standard-deviation error bars. PEQ uses all 112 designed couplings. At $p_{\mathrm{c}}=0.5$ , the 56th coupling determines the cutoff $\alpha^{*}$ , marked with a green circle, and PEQ $=0.42$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Measured two-qubit conditional negativities across the 64-qubit square-lattice processor and the sorted distribution of edge negativities used to evaluate PEQ at the bond-percolation threshold.

fields.result: Formulates reference-assisted qutrit control for charge-$4e$ superconductors under sector preservation and same-label covariance. Proves record probabilities are independent of reference state inside sector span $S_{R}=\operatorname{span}\{\lvert 1\rangle_{R},\lvert 2\rangle_{R}\}$ for charge-conjugation-invariant inputs, yielding an accepted-run target infidelity bounded by $e_{N}+r_{\nu}+r_{m}+r_{\gamma}$.
fields.question: What operational conditions and error budgets govern reference-assisted qutrit control and conditional distillation using charge-$4e$ parafermionic zero modes?
fields.limits: Requires sector-preserving instruments, same-label covariance, and accepted-run conditioning. Ignores native charge-$4e$ extraction circuits, device thresholds, correlated Markov drift, and thermal quasiparticle leakage.

fields.result: FPGA-based QDPU architecture classifies a $50\times 50$ atom array in 12.5 $\mu$s using one matched-filter lane. Eliminating an assumed 150 ms host round trip increases simulated $35\times 35$ target assembly success from 8% to 85% and cuts wall-clock time per assembly from 19 s to 0.16 s.
fields.question: How can classical measurement processing and rearrangement feedback be architected to meet tight real-time latency budgets in scaling neutral-atom quantum processors?
fields.limits: Simulated atom-loss model assumes 60 s trap lifetime and 0.1% loss per moved atom; CNN detector for $10^4$ sites exceeds DSP limits on the target device.
tools: AMD Zynq UltraScale+ RFSoC (xczu49dr on ZCU216)
NVIDIA DGX Spark over 10 GbE NVQLink
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12: Assembly success against the host round-trip $t_{\mathrm{host}}$ added to every cycle, at four trap lifetimes [phys] : matched filter at $10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ (solid, markers at the simulated round-trips; the $150\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ point at its own operating exposure of $11\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ ) and, for comparison, the CNN at $10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s}$ on one FPGA core with no host (dashed, same shade). $50\times 50$ array, centred $35\times 35$ target, $60\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ fill, no refill, at most nine cycles per attempt, $0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}$ loss per moved atom, $1000$ attempts per point. $\tau_{\mathrm{vac}}=$1380\text{\,}\mathrm{s}$$ is the $23\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{i}\mathrm{n}$ lifetime of [ 10 ] .

fields.result: Spin-completed post-processing of qDRIFT measurement samples eliminates spin contamination, giving subspace roots with spin error $|⟨\hat{S}^{2}⟩-S(S+1)| < 10^{-11}$. On an IBM Heron processor, it matches Cartesian post-processing accuracy while reducing diagonalized subspace dimensions by two to three orders of magnitude.
fields.question: How can spin symmetry be incorporated into sample-based quantum diagonalization pipelines based on randomized time evolution?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on active spaces up to (32e, 24o). Spin completion requires enumerating all open-shell spin couplings for sampled configurations, which scales exponentially with the count of singly occupied orbitals.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Spin energetics of the oxo- Mn (Salen) molecular compound (hardware). Energy error $|E-E_{\mathrm{DMRG}}|$ (a–c) and spin error $|\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle-S(S+1)|$ (d–f) against the subspace dimension, for the singlet, triplet, and quintet states, computed in the $M_{S}=0$ , 1, and 2 sectors, respectively, in the (32e, 24o) active space. Marker shape denotes the subspace construction and color the number of excitations ( $N=\{5,10,15\}$ ); HCI and its spin-adapted variant (see main text and Appendix C ) are shown as references in red. The dashed line marks chemical accuracy ( $1.6\text{\,}\mathrm{mHa}$ ). Classical and quantum spin-complete errors are omitted from the plot, as their values are substantially lower than those of the other methods (machine precision).
fields.figure_gloss: Energy error relative to DMRG (top) and total spin deviation $|\langle\hat{S}^{2}\rangle - S(S+1)|$ (bottom) versus diagonalized subspace dimension for singlet, triplet, and quintet states of oxo-Mn(Salen). Spin completion maintains exact spin purity and reaches target energy accuracy with subspaces two to three orders of magnitude smaller than Cartesian post-processing.

fields.result: Simulated $Y_{\pi/2}$ coherent-control infidelity falls below $10^{-4}$ with computational subspace leakage suppressed via DRAG-inspired framing ramps, requiring only a 16-bit stored ramp sequence and 223 Josephson junctions.
fields.question: Can coherent errors and leakage intrinsic to discrete SFQ transmon control be suppressed to the level of high-fidelity microwave control while drastically cutting cryogenic memory overhead?
fields.prior: Full SFQ arbitrary sequences required storing hundreds of pulses, while experimental multichip SFQ control had Clifford errors around 1.2(1)% (Liu 2023) and on-chip digital control achieved 99% to 99.9% fidelity (Kang 2024).
fields.limits: Purely coherent unitary simulations; ignores relaxation ($T_{1}$), dephasing ($T_{2}$), and quasiparticle poisoning. Complete circuit-level timing-closure and layout margins not analyzed.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Comparison of three SFQ control schemes for the target $Y_{\pi/2}$ gate: (a) regular sequence without ramps, (b) combined sequence with symmetric ramps and (c) combined sequence with independently optimized ramps. First row: evolution from the initial state $\ket{z+}=\ket{0}$ , illustrating the intended $\pi/2$ rotation through the evolution toward equal $\ket{0}$ and $\ket{1}$ populations. Second row: evolution from the initial state $\ket{y+}$ . Since $\ket{y+}$ is an eigenstate of the $Y$ rotation axis, an ideal $Y_{\pi/2}$ gate leaves its computational-basis populations equal to $1/2$ ; deviations therefore highlight the additional effects of the control sequence and, in panels (b) and (c), the short ramp corrections. Third row: population $W_{2}$ of the first leakage level for the $\ket{y+}$ initial state. Bottom row: spectra of the corresponding SFQ control signals. The solid vertical line indicates the qubit transition frequency $\omega_{01}$ and the dashed vertical line the leakage transition frequency $\omega_{12}$ . The infidelity shown below each column is the leakage-inclusive average gate infidelity calculated over all six cardinal input states according to Eq. ( 7 ), rather than from either of the individual trajectories displayed here. The rapid changes near the boundaries of panels (b) and (c) correspond to the short on- and off-ramp sequences generated on the $40~\mathrm{GHz}$ timing grid.
fields.figure_gloss: State evolution and pulse trains for $Y_{\pi/2}$ gates using unramped, symmetric-ramped, and independently optimized ramped SFQ sequences, demonstrating leakage elimination into state $\ket{2}$.

fields.result: Steady-state populations within the loss cascade scale inversely with Fock number as $P_{n}^{\mathrm{ss}} = J_{\mathrm{G}}^{\mathrm{ss}}/(n\kappa_{c})$ under global multi-quantum replenishment, while an engineered local transition enhances target state $\ket{R}$ via population current $J_{\mathrm{L}}^{\mathrm{ss}}(R)$.
fields.question: Can autonomous Fock-state stabilization in open bosonic systems be unified under a common physical mechanism across different microscopic reservoir engineering processes?
fields.limits: Spectrally selective regime where non-resonant transitions are strongly suppressed ($K_c \gg \kappa_c$ or $\chi_s \gg \kappa_c$), zero-temperature bath, theoretical derivations and numerical simulations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Common harmonic Fock-state populations generated by selective global connections. a–c, Kerr-resolved global implementations: (a) pumped $N_{s}$ -quantum JC, (b) relaxation-assisted $N_{s}$ -quantum AJC, and (c) a coherent $N_{s}$ -quantum drive. d, e, Dispersively resolved counterparts of (a, b), respectively. The upper (lower) row in each panel corresponds to $N_{s}=3$ ( $N_{s}=6$ ). The Wigner functions (left) are computed numerically from the reduced bosonic steady states obtained by solving the full microscopic Lindblad master equations; the corresponding Fock-state populations are shown on the right. Blue bars show full microscopic Lindblad results, red open circles the analytical effective-current predictions, and black dashed curves the reference $P_{1}^{\mathrm{num}}/n$ , where $P_{1}^{\mathrm{num}}$ is the numerically obtained population at $n=1$ . The reference curves are extended beyond $N_{s}$ only as a guide. The ideal analytical populations vanish for $n>N_{s}$ . All Wigner functions use the same linear color scale, $[-2/\pi,2/\pi]$ . No local connector is applied. The global coupling strengths satisfy $g_{G,\mathrm{JC}}^{(N_{s})}/\kappa_{c}=g_{G,\mathrm{AJC}}^{(N_{s})}/\kappa_{c}=g_{G,\mathrm{drv}}^{(N_{s})}/\kappa_{c}=5$ . The pumped-JC cases (a, d) use $\wp_{s}/\kappa_{c}=100$ and $\gamma_{s}/\kappa_{c}=1$ ; the AJC cases (b, e) use $(\wp_{s},\gamma_{s})/\kappa_{c}=(0,100)$ . For (a–c), $K_{c}/\kappa_{c}=10^{4}$ and $\Delta_{c}/\kappa_{c}=-10^{4}N_{s}$ , with $\Delta_{s}=0$ in (a, b). For (d, e), $K_{c}=\Delta_{c}=0$ , $\chi_{s}/\kappa_{c}=3\times 10^{4}$ and $\Delta_{s}/\kappa_{c}=-3\times 10^{4}N_{s}$ . These choices place the selected global transitions on resonance.
fields.figure_gloss: Steady-state Fock distributions and Wigner functions for three global connector implementations across Kerr- and dispersively resolved regimes. Bars show numerical master equation results agreeing with the predicted $1/n$ scaling (open circles and dashed curves) for $n \leq N_s$.

fields.result: Explicit normalized block-encoding of the shifted global stiffness matrix for 2D isotropic linear elasticity using a constant number of ancillae and logarithmic gate complexity in the degrees of freedom ($44(n_x+n_y)+156$ Hadamard, $48(n_x+n_y)+278$ CNOT, $106(n_x+n_y)+341$ $\mathrm{T}$, and $64$ $\mathrm{R}_y$ gates). Enables QSVT-based linear equation solving scaling as $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa})$.
fields.question: Can finite element stiffness matrices for isotropic linear elasticity be efficiently block-encoded in a normalized, shifted form to enable square-root condition-number scaling $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa})$ in quantum linear system algorithms?
fields.prior: Existing quantum finite element methods block-encode standard operators with query complexity linear in the condition number $\kappa$, whereas optimal positive-definite quantum solvers require normalized block-encodings of shifted operators (Orsucci and Dunjko 2021) which are not directly provided by standard block-encodings.
fields.limits: Restricted to 2D isotropic linear elastic materials on uniform rectangular meshes; requires condition number bounds or heuristic extrapolation to set polynomial degree; boundary and material oracles excluded from core gate count.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Quantum circuit for the normalized block encoding $U_{B}=U_{L}^{\dagger}R_{L,\mathrm{out}}U_{L}$ . Here, $n:=n_{x}+n_{y}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit schematic implementing the normalized block encoding $\mathbf{U}_B = \mathbf{U}_L^\dagger \mathbf{R}_{L,\text{out}} \mathbf{U}_L$ for the shifted stiffness matrix, displaying register allocations across $n = n_x + n_y$ system qubits and auxiliary registers.

fields.result: Synthesizes quantum block-encoding circuits directly from matrix entry formulas, matching or beating 37 of 39 published baselines and improving subnormalization by up to $10{,}487\times$ in under 5 seconds for dimensions exceeding $2^{100}$.
fields.question: Can quantum block-encoding circuits be automatically synthesized with poly-logarithmic cost directly from mathematical entry formulas rather than designed by hand?
fields.prior: Hand-crafted circuits or explicit entry enumeration like FABLE (Camps and Van Beeumen 2022), which incurs $O(N^2)$ gates and cannot scale past dimension $\sim 2^{12} \times 2^{12}$.
fields.limits: Counts in Clifford+$T$+$R_z$ gate set, treating arbitrary $R_z$ gates as incurring $O(\log(1/\epsilon))$ $T$ gates. Hand-written rewrite rules capped at an intermediate representation size of $10^5$ nodes.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12 . Breakdown of MARBLE compile time as the matrix dimension $N$ ( $x$ -axis) grows.
fields.figure_gloss: Total MARBLE compile time (seconds) on the y-axis broken down by phase across matrix dimension $N$ up to $2^{100}$ on the x-axis for three benchmark matrices. Circuit optimization time remains flat, keeping total execution under 5 seconds.

fields.result: Extending a generalized Dicke state of $(j-1)$ particle registers of $n_{qb}$ qubits each by one mode uses $\mathcal{O}(j\log_2^2 j + j n_{qb})$ CNOT and single-qubit gates, using $3j+\lceil\log_2 j\rceil+\mathcal{O}(\max(n_{qb},\log_2 j))$ clean ancillae.
fields.question: How can quantum registers be iteratively symmetrized and antisymmetrized particle-by-particle with reduced asymptotic gate complexity in the presence of repeated bosonic modes?
fields.prior: Appendix A of Gálvez-Viruet et al. (2024), scaling worse by nearly two powers of $j$.
fields.limits: Subcompetitive against Jordan-Wigner encoding in the saturation regime where particle number approaches mode count. Analysis covers gate counts rather than circuit depth.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Multicontrolled operation to store the positions of the $\alpha$ mode in register $B$ . Qubit $B_{i}$ is flipped to $\ket{1}$ when sub-register $A_{i}$ stores mode $\ket{\alpha}$ . Notation: the $\bullet^{\alpha}$ denotes conditioning on the multi-qubits state $\ket{\alpha}$ rather than in a single qubit state $\ket{1}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Quantum circuit mapping occupied sub-registers $A_i$ matching mode $\ket{\alpha}$ into flag bits in auxiliary register $B$ using multicontrolled bit flips.

fields.result: A symmetry-breaking impurity in a charged dual-unitary quantum circuit generates persistent, non-vanishing stationary entanglement negativity and mutual information between intervals straddling the defect. It also violates the standard integrable identity $\mathcal{E}_{A_{1}:A_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}{\cal I}^{(1/2)}_{A_{1}:A_{2}}$.
fields.question: How is non-equilibrium local relaxation and entanglement dynamics modified by a spatially fixed quantum impurity that breaks a global bulk symmetry outside the observed subsystem?
fields.prior: In uncharged dual-unitary circuits or standard translation-invariant quenches, steady-state mutual information and negativity between separated intervals decay to zero, and the negativity satisfies $\mathcal{E}_{A_{1}:A_{2}}=\frac{1}{2}{\cal I}^{(1/2)}_{A_{1}:A_{2}}$.
fields.limits: Analytic derivations assume brickwork dual-unitary gates with chiral $U(1)\otimes U(1)$ symmetry, homogeneous initial states, and bulk dynamics either strictly non-interacting/integrable or chaotic (membrane picture).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 12: The long-time limits of the entanglement negativity and of the $n=1/2$ Rényi mutual information between two intervals in a charged dual-unitary circuit with an impurity $U_{\rm XY}(\gamma)$ , as defined in Eq. ( 2.45 ). The local charge-sector dimension is $d=3$ , and the half-lengths of the intervals $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are fixed at $\ell=20$ . The results are shown for an initial state with $\theta=0.2$ and as a function of the impurity parameter $\gamma$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Long-time asymptotic entanglement negativity $\mathcal{E}_{A_1:A_2}(\infty)$ and half Rényi mutual information $\frac{1}{2}\mathcal{I}_{A_1:A_2}^{(1/2)}(\infty)$ as a function of impurity parameter $\gamma$. Non-zero steady-state values persist across intermediate $\gamma$, and the two curves diverge, breaking the standard integrable equivalence.

fields.result: Ground-state extrapolation to zero energy variance per site gives nonzero charge-density-wave order $m_0=0.002213(14)$ in the half-filled $1/d$ Coulomb chain at weak coupling $V=2$, with variational energy variance down to $2\times 10^{-10}$.
fields.question: Can matrix product state algorithms compute thermodynamic-limit ground states, excitation spectra, and energy variances for algebraically decaying long-range interactions without fitting interactions to sums of exponentials?
fields.prior: Numerical DMRG on rings up to 28 sites found a quasimetallic phase and could not resolve charge order at weak coupling (Capponi et al. 2004), placing weak coupling on the metallic side.
fields.limits: One-dimensional translation-invariant systems in the thermodynamic limit; assumes pairwise interactions.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: The energy and CDW amplitude for the half-filled Coulomb chain, extrapolated to zero variance for $V=2$ (left) and $V=4$ (right). (a,b) Energy per site $e$ as a function of the energy variance $v$ , with the fit $e=e_{0}+av$ and the extrapolated values $e_{0}=-0.863815982983(15)$ and $-1.1121016662500(7)$ , respectively. (c,d) CDW amplitude $m_{\rm CDW}$ as a function of $v^{p}$ , with the fit $m_{\rm CDW}=m_{0}+bv^{p}$ and the extrapolated values $m_{0}=0.002213(14)$ and $0.09923211059(3)$ , respectively. In panels (a), (b), and (d), the extrapolated values $e_{0}$ and $m_{0}$ are subtracted. The fitted exponent $p$ is given in panels (c) and (d), and the point with $\chi=3072$ is marked in panel (c). Plus signs show the numerical results, and black crosses with error bars indicate the extrapolated values. Gray symbols ( $\chi=256$ and 384 at $V=2$ ) are not included in the fit and lie outside the range of panel (a). Lines show fits to the data for $\chi=512$ –3072 at $V=2$ and 256–640 at $V=4$ . Numbers in parentheses indicate $1\sigma$ fit uncertainties in the last quoted digits.
fields.figure_gloss: Energy per site $e$ and charge-density-wave order parameter $m_{\rm CDW}$ plotted against energy variance per site $v$ for $V=2$ and $V=4$. Extrapolations to $v\to 0$ show finite charge order persisting down to $V=2$.

fields.result: Joint optimization of a single-site interpolating operator and a single-particle momentum superposition yields localized excitations that prepare wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent from the interacting vacuum, avoiding ansatz-dependent barren plateaus.
fields.question: How can asymptotic incoming particle wave packets of arbitrary spatial extent be prepared accurately directly from the interacting vacuum in lattice field theories?
fields.prior: Localized single-particle excitations previously required optimizing norm of excitation tensors, excess energy density with variational phases, or an ansatz for preparation circuits.
fields.limits: (1+1)-dimensional $\phi^4$ scalar field theory, single-site interpolating operator support, digitized local field space.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Localized excitation and scalable wave packet preparation for $\tilde{\lambda}_{0}=0.8$ , $\tilde{m}_{0}=0.1$ , $d=8$ and $\phi_{\text{max}}=2.9$ . (Left) Leading and subleading eigenmodes of momentum space profile $h(\tilde{k})$ , with their corresponding infidelities. Teal curves plot $h_{\tilde{m}}(\tilde{k})$ for $\tilde{m}=0.03$ to $0.83$ and $\delta\tilde{m}=0.2$ , with increasing transparency for larger masses. (Middle) Infidelity $1-\mathcal{F}$ as a function of $\tilde{m}$ for momentum space profile $h_{\tilde{m}_{\text{phy}}}(\tilde{k})$ and interpolating operators supported on $[n=1,2,3]$ sites. Solid and dashed curves denote default and search procedures for selecting the tolerance of pseudoinverse. The vertical dashed line indicates the mass parameter $\tilde{m}$ that minimizes the infidelity. The momentum space superposition profile for localized excitation preserves reflection symmetry about the origin. The $[n=2]$ case corresponds to an operator supported on the site at the origin and one adjacent site, while the $[n=3]$ case corresponds to an operator supported on three consecutive sites symmetrically arranged about the origin. (Right) Infidelity of single particle momentum eigenstates constructed using interpolating operators. Reference states are computed with two-site excitation tensors.
fields.figure_gloss: Eigenmodes of the wave packet momentum space profile $h(\tilde{k})$ (left) and spatial profiles of the resulting localized excitation and wide wave packet prepared from the interacting vacuum (right). Infidelity is plotted against system size.

fields.result: Subgap Andreev transport in transmon-scale $\mathrm{Al/AlO_x/Al}$ junctions is non-ergodic and dominated by $\lesssim 300$ leaky channels with transparencies orders of magnitude above the ideal tunneling limit $\lesssim 10^{-6}$. For small or high-aspect-ratio junctions, effective transparency $\tau_e$ grows with area instead of averaging out, peaking near $A_{\mathrm{jj}} \approx 0.15~\mu\mathrm{m}^2$ before decaying as $A_{\mathrm{jj}}^{-1}$ above a threshold length scale.
fields.question: Does the transparency distribution of $\mathrm{Al/AlO_x/Al}$ Josephson junctions self-average with junction area, ensuring an area-independent current-phase skew?
fields.prior: Assumed constant and independent of area $A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ when isolating higher Josephson harmonics from circuit inductance in transmons.
fields.limits: Measured on 134 devices at $T = 10\text{ mK}$ in the zero-temperature limit $k_B T \ll \Delta$; $\sigma_{\mathrm{II}} \lesssim 0.14\text{ nm}$ is bounded algebraically from above rather than uniquely resolved.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Normal-state conductance, effective transparency ( $\tau_{e}=I_{2}/I_{1}$ ) and effective channel number ( $N_{e}$ ) versus junction area for the high-aspect-ratio (HAR) sets ( a - c ) and Square Set A ( d - f ). a , d , $G_{n}$ versus $A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ . HAR Sets A and B have a short dimension of either $l=200$ nm or $l=300$ nm and correspond to different fabrication batches while set C varies both $l$ and $w$ . Square Set A comprises four oxidation exposures (15, 30, 120, and 240 Torr $\cdot$ min). Dashed lines are one-parameter fits $G_{n}=C\,A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ ( $\propto A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ ) to each series. Insets: false-color SEM images of a representative HAR and square junction with the electrode widths $l$ , $w$ marked (scale bars 500 nm). b , e , $\tau_{e}$ versus $A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ . $\tau_{e}$ was previously assumed to be constant with junction area [ 21 ] . Here it increases with area in every HAR set, whereas the square junctions are non-monotonic with peak near $A_{\mathrm{jj}}\approx 0.15~\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}$ . Large junctions show decreasing $\tau_{e}$ as $\propto A_{\mathrm{jj}}^{-1}$ (dashed guide). c , f , Point-wise $N_{e}$ (Eq. 3 ) versus $A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ . The HAR samples show a strongly sublinear $N_{e}$ , while square devices have constant $N_{e}\approx 50$ for $A_{\mathrm{jj}}<0.15~\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}$ and then $N_{e}=(3.3\pm 0.2)\times 10^{3}\,A_{\mathrm{jj}}^{2.07\pm 0.07}$ ( $A_{\mathrm{jj}}$ in $\mu\mathrm{m}^{2}$ ) for larger junctions ( $\propto A_{\mathrm{jj}}^{2}$ , dashed guide). Insets: $\tau_{e}$ versus $G_{n}$ for junctions with $G_{n}<100~\mu\mathrm{S}$ . Independent of oxidation condition, the points are collinear with inverse slope corresponding to a constant $N_{e}=274\pm 5$ (fit to HAR Sets A and B) and $N_{e}=47\pm 4$ (Square Set A, solid).
fields.figure_gloss: Measured normal-state conductance $G_n$, effective transparency $\tau_e = I_2/I_1$, and effective channel number $N_e$ versus junction area $A_{\mathrm{jj}}$. Unlike linear $G_n$, $\tau_e$ increases monotonically with area for high-aspect-ratio junctions and peaks non-monotonically near $0.15~\mu\mathrm{m}^2$ for square junctions before scaling downward as $A_{\mathrm{jj}}^{-1}$.

fields.result: Gradients avoid barren plateaus if $\rho^{\otimes 2}$ and $\mathcal{M}^{\otimes 2}$ concentrate on the same irreducible invariant subspace of polynomial dimension moved inverse-polynomially by the differentiated gate. For an $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ ansatz with non-algebra observable $X^{(1)}X^{(2)}$, variance decays as $2/n^{2}$, matching the exact formula $(2n^3 - 3n - 2)/(n^2(n-1)(n+1)^2)$.
fields.question: Does a given parameterized quantum circuit necessarily induce a barren plateau for arbitrary states and observables?
fields.prior: Lie-algebraic frameworks assume the observable is generated by the circuit's Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$; for $X^{(1)}X^{(2)}$ under number-conserving fermionic circuits, this accounted for only $56\%$ of gradient variance at $n=4$ and $50\%$ asymptotically.
fields.limits: Bounds are generally not tight. Requires circuit segments on both sides of the differentiated gate to form $2$-designs for exact variance; sampling relative precision requires exponential runs if variance is exponentially small.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Variance of $\partial_{\theta_{\ell,1}}C$ for the $\mathrm{SU}(n)$ compound ansatz, $n=4,\dots,20$ . Setting. $G=\mathrm{SU}(n)$ acts on ${\mathcal{H}}=(\mathbb{C}^{2})^{\otimes n}\cong\bigoplus_{m=0}^{n}\Lambda^{m}(\mathbb{C}^{n})$ through the compound representation $\Pi(V)=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{n}C_{m}(V)$ , where the $m$ -th compound matrix $C_{m}(V)$ acts on the Hamming-weight- $m$ subspace; equivalently $\pi_{*}(X)=\sum_{a,b}X_{ab}\,a_{a}^{\dagger}a_{b}$ with Jordan–Wigner operators $a_{a}=Z_{1}\cdots Z_{a-1}\,|0\rangle\langle 1|_{a}$ . The ansatz ( 4 ) is $U(\bm{\theta})=\prod_{l=1}^{L}\prod_{j=1}^{n^{2}-1}\exp\!\big(\theta_{l,j}\,\pi_{*}(g_{j})\big)$ with $\theta_{l,j}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[-\pi,\pi]$ and the basis $\{g_{j}\}=\{-i(E_{pq}+E_{qp}),\,E_{pq}-E_{qp}\}_{p Curves. Solid line: exact variance $\mathrm{Var}(n)=\frac{2n^{3}-3n-2}{n^{2}(n-1)(n+1)^{2}}\approx 2/n^{2}$ of Equation 21 , derived in Supplementary Section S8.5 . Dashed line: its first term $\frac{n}{(n-1)(n+1)^{2}}$ , the contribution of the component of ${\mathcal{M}}$ inside the algebra, which is all that the Lie-algebraic formula accounts for. Squares: Case-3 lower bound Equation 12 . Circles: output of Algorithm 1 in its exact form, with the four-term shift rule for $H$ ( $\gamma=2$ ), $\delta=10^{-3}$ and $\widetilde{\varepsilon}=0.999/n^{2}$ , using $\mathcal{N}=\lceil 32\ln(2/\delta)/\widetilde{\varepsilon}^{2}\rceil$ runs ( $6.2\times 10^{4}$ at $n=4$ to $3.9\times 10^{7}$ at $n=20$ ; the finite-difference form needs $4.6\times 10^{8}$ to $1.8\times 10^{14}$ runs for the same guarantee). Every run was simulated, with the value of the cost function at each shift computed in a time polynomial in $n$ as described in Supplementary Section S8.5 . Error bars: the certified accuracy $\pm\widetilde{\varepsilon}=\pm 0.999/n^{2}$ , guaranteed with probability at least $1-\delta=0.999$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Gradient variance versus number of qubits $n$ from $4$ to $20$. Solid line shows the exact analytical variance $(2n^3 - 3n - 2)/(n^2(n-1)(n+1)^2)$ decaying as $2/n^2$, compared against the analytical lower bound and circuit run estimates.

fields.result: A single qubit achieves success probability $\mathcal{P}_{Q}^{\max} = \frac{1}{3}(1 + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \approx 0.62$, strictly beating the classical c-bit bound $\mathcal{P}_{C}^{\max} \approx 0.58$, in the Holevo–Frenkel–Weiner framework with parity-concealment constraints.
fields.question: Can a qubit outperform a classical bit in the Holevo–Frenkel–Weiner communication scenario with unbounded shared randomness and without entanglement or measurement incompatibility?
fields.prior: Frenkel and Weiner (2015) showed that with unbounded shared randomness and no Bob input, every qubit strategy can be simulated by a c-bit.
fields.limits: Requires parity concealment constraints to hold for every individual realization of shared randomness, not just on average.
fields.figure_gloss: Comparison of quantum success probability and POVM-based relative entropy of coherence $C_{rel}(\mathbb{I}/2, \mathbb{M})$ as functions of Bob's measurement parameters $\alpha_b$, showing both peak at the trine POVM where $\alpha_b = 2/3$.

fields.result: Discovered type-II band alignment and magnetic proximity coupling in $\mathrm{WS_2}/\mathrm{CrSBr}$ heterostructures, yielding enhanced Zeeman valley splitting and spin-selective interlayer charge transfer dependent on relative spin-valley polarization and $\mathrm{CrSBr}$ magnetization.
fields.question: How do magnetic order and anisotropic electronic dispersion in $\mathrm{CrSBr}$ couple to valley excitons in monolayer $\mathrm{WS_2}$?
fields.limits: Dependent on twist angle and relative alignment between valley-spin polarization and magnetic substrate.

fields.result: Optical rectification of a 100 fs laser pulse inside a KTP crystal generates a quasi-DC field yielding an electric Aharonov-Bohm phase $\phi_{AB} = \pi$ at laser intensity $I_{0} \approx 4.3 \times 10^{8}\text{ W/cm}^{2}$. The residual field inside the slit apertures is an order of magnitude smaller and displaces only the diffraction envelope without shifting the fringes.
fields.question: Can the electric Aharonov-Bohm effect be observed for free electrons traversing paths with negligible local electric fields?
fields.limits: Theoretical calculation in the paraxial approximation. Assumes electron position changes negligibly during the 100 fs pulse passage.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Interference patterns calculated within the paraxial approximation, $k_{y}=k_{e}y/D$ , with $\tilde{\psi}_{0}(k_{y})\propto 2J_{1}(k_{y}R)/(k_{y}R)$ for a circular aperture. In both panels, $D=10$ cm, $T=100$ fs, $d=3~\mu$ m $w_{0}=1~\mu$ m $k_{e}=1.15\times 10^{11}$ m -1 , corresponding to 500 eV electrons. (a) Effect of the residual field for different slab widths $L_{x}$ , excluding the AB phase. The curves, obtained from Eq. ( 16 ), correspond to $\delta k=0$ (black), $L_{x}=20~\mu$ m (blue), $10~\mu$ m (yellow), and $5~\mu$ m (green). The laser intensity is $I_{0}=3.5\times 10^{8}$ W/cm 2 , corresponding to $\phi_{\rm AB}=\pi$ . (b) Full interference pattern including both the dynamical momentum shift due to the residual field and the AB phase, with $L_{x}=20\mu$ m. The dashed black curve corresponds to $I_{0}=0$ , while the solid red, and blue curves correspond, respectively, to $I_{0}=4.3\times 10^{8}$ , and $8.6\times 10^{8}$ W/cm 2 , yielding $\phi_{\rm AB}=\pi$ , and $2\pi$ .
