fields.result: Surveys the end-to-end QRNG pipeline across discrete-variable and continuous-variable sources, highlighting CV throughput gains via broadband optical signals and multi-bit digitization versus DV constraints from detector dead time and afterpulsing.
fields.question: What is the complete state-of-the-art landscape, performance comparison, and theoretical-to-hardware pipeline for quantum random number generators across physical entropy sources?
fields.limits: Dependent on reliable classical-to-quantum noise separation, finite-size security analyses, trust models (device-independent to characterized), and distinguishing offline from real-time generation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8 : Generation rates of surveyed DV-QRNGs (left) and CV-QRNGs (right), grouped by entropy source.
fields.figure_gloss: Comparison of generation rates across different physical entropy sources for discrete-variable (DV) and continuous-variable (CV) QRNG architectures reported in the literature.

fields.result: Structure-preserving error mitigation restores parameter-dependent feature gradients without per-step recalibration, matching noiseless variational minimization to within $\sim 628{,}000$ total shots versus $16{,}500{,}000$ for Clifford data regression, and scales to 100 aggregate qubits across 25 parallel four-qubit channels.
fields.question: How can circuit-induced distortions of quantum neural network features be mitigated across evolving circuit parameters without recalibrating or executing auxiliary circuits at every training step?
fields.prior: Clifford data regression (CDR) required fitting auxiliary near-Clifford circuits at every evaluation (16,500,000 shots at 500 evaluations), zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) required 1,500,000 shots, and standard readout mitigation failed to correct circuit-execution noise.
fields.limits: Requires $2^N$ computational-basis inputs per $N$-qubit channel ($N=4$ tested), restricting channel width. Assumes channel noise responses are compatible and remain stable over training duration.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Reusable calibration improves variational optimization. (a) Minimum magnetization $\mathcal{C}_{Z}=\langle Z\rangle$ [Eq. ( 11 )] reached during optimization as a function of the CZ-gate error probability. Mitigation keeps the optimized magnetization close to the ideal minimum of $-1$ across the simulated noise range. (b) Experimental optimization trajectories on an IBM quantum processor. After 150 optimization steps, the mitigated magnetization reaches $-0.86$ , compared with $-0.42$ without mitigation. Teal solid and orange dashed curves denote mitigated and unmitigated results, respectively. (c) A fixed calibration brings training close to the noiseless reference, yielding the closest final mean training objective among the noisy protocols tested: $\mathcal{C}_{Z}=-0.953$ versus $-0.958$ in the noiseless control. The dark blue dashed line with open circles denotes noiseless training; the teal solid line with filled diamonds denotes structure-preserving error mitigation. The inset magnifies the unsmoothed mean trajectories of these two methods over steps 350–500. Other curves show unmitigated training, readout mitigation, zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE), and Clifford data regression (CDR). All conditions use the same objective and zero initial angles, with at most 500 objective evaluations per run. Noisy conditions use the CZ-associated error parameter $e_{2}=0.006$ and a readout-flip probability of $0.01$ . Curves show the mean over five independent finite-shot repeats; shaded bands in the main panel indicate one sample standard deviation. Simulations in (a,c) use five qubits and four circuit layers. Protocol details and measurement budgets are given in Appendix S3.S3.8 .
fields.figure_gloss: Normalized mean magnetization versus objective evaluation count during variational minimization under gate and measurement noise. The precalibrated estimator tracks noiseless optimization using 628,000 shots, outperforming readout mitigation and zero-noise extrapolation while avoiding the 16.5M-shot overhead of CDR.

fields.result: Continuous-unitary-design-inspired dynamical decoupling (CUDD) eliminates first-order static noise during finite-duration pulses by concatenating continuous unitary design trajectories, outperforming CPMG, XY4, and UR4 against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning.
fields.question: Can dynamical decoupling achieve universal decoupling and control-error robustness under realistic finite-duration pulses without assuming instantaneous bang-bang control?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on single qubits with 1 ns waveform resolution; assumes static noise during continuous segments and piecewise-constant control parameters.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Experimental comparison of the robust CUDD sequence and conventional DD sequences in the presence of Rabi errors and detuning on $Q_{4}$ , with $\tau=60$ ns. The coherence protection efficiency $\eta$ is defined as the ratio of the integrated coherent signal of a given DD sequence to that of the free evolution, with both signals measured relative to the 0.5 baseline.
fields.figure_gloss: Coherence protection efficiency $\eta$ plotted against injected Rabi errors and detuning offsets on superconducting qubit $Q_{4}$ at pulse interval $\tau = 60$ ns. CUDD maintains higher protection efficiency over wider error ranges than CPMG, XY4, and UR4 sequences.

fields.result: Noise-aware test oracle matches nominal false-positive rate at 0.0011 for $\alpha=10^{-3}$ over 9,000 correct simulation runs while attaining 0.941 F1 on non-equivalent injected faults. On an IBM Heron device, it rejected 0 of 82 correct runs and detected 120 of 121 faults and semantic mutants.
fields.question: How can a NISQ quantum testing framework provide a test oracle with a controlled false-positive rate under noise without relying on noiseless simulators or global tolerances?
fields.prior: Fixed-threshold oracles had 36–74% false-positive rates, a QOIN-style filter had 8.9%, and globally noise-calibrated thresholds had 10.8%.
fields.limits: Requires $\ge 16$ shots per observed outcome for reliable control; vulnerable to undetected device drift; attribution of noise effects fails at high noise regimes; does not support mid-circuit measurements or dynamic circuits.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3 . RQ1: false-positive rate of each oracle on $9{,}000$ correct runs (point: observed rate; bar: 95% cluster-bootstrap interval over calibration windows; log scale). The dashed and dotted lines mark the nominal levels $\alpha=10^{-3}$ and $10^{-2}$ . An arrow marks an interval whose lower bound is $0$ , which a log scale cannot show (SPC envelope: $3$ false positives, interval $[0,0.0008]$ ). Horizontal interval plot on a logarithmic axis of the false-positive rate of each oracle on correct programs. NAO and NAO-1 lie near the nominal levels 0.001 and 0.01, the SPC envelope lies below them, the QOIN-style filter near 0.09, and the fixed thresholds between 0.36 and 0.74.
fields.figure_gloss: False-positive rate across different test oracles over 9,000 correct runs on a log scale with 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals. Shows that the proposed noise-aware oracle aligns with the nominal levels $\alpha=10^{-3}$ and $\alpha=10^{-2}$, whereas fixed, filtered, and globally calibrated thresholds yield high error rates.

fields.result: Cryostat input line attenuation at 6.0 GHz is measured as $(74.7\pm 0.2)\text{ dB}$ using directly coupled transmons and $(75.4\pm 6.8)\text{ dB}$ using dispersively coupled transmons. Directly coupled qubits sense from $-155\text{ dBm}$ to $-130\text{ dBm}$; dispersively coupled qubits access $-95\text{ dBm}$ to $-55\text{ dBm}$.
fields.question: Can the AC Stark shift on dispersively coupled transmons achieve quantitative microwave power sensing at millikelvin temperatures, and how does its accuracy compare with resonant wave scattering on directly coupled transmons?
fields.limits: Direct coupling requires the qubit to be tuned into resonance with the signal. Dispersive coupling uncertainty is dominated by numerical modeling errors of the feedline-to-resonator transfer function.
tools: electromagnetic and circuit co-simulation (Sonnet and uSimmics)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Comparison of power sensing using LP and HP qubits. (a) Line attenuation obtained from LP qubit measurements at $6.0\hskip 1.42271pt\mathrm{GHz}$ (left) and at their flux sweet spots between $6.8\hskip 1.42271pt\mathrm{GHz}$ and $6.9\hskip 1.42271pt\mathrm{GHz}$ (right). (b) Line attenuation obtained from HP qubit measurements at $6.0\hskip 1.42271pt\mathrm{GHz}$ (left) and at $8.0\hskip 1.42271pt\mathrm{GHz}$ (right). For each panel, the grey dashed line indicates the mean and the grey region the uncertainty of the mean derived from the three individual qubit measurements.
fields.figure_gloss: Line attenuation estimates and uncertainties determined for three directly coupled transmons and three dispersively coupled transmons at 6.0 GHz and near flux sweet spots (6.8–8.0 GHz).

fields.result: Capacitor-based analog-memory AWG generates 40 Msps Gaussian pulses at 14 K with 50 ksps programming rate and no measurable voltage decay over 2 s; room-temperature prototype reaches 160 Msps.
fields.question: Can high-speed arbitrary waveform generation for cryogenic qubit control be decoupled from high-speed digital-to-analog conversion using local analog memory?
fields.limits: Total power consumption unmeasured. Cryogenic prototype has 10 memory cells and exhibits crosstalk voltage spikes via FPC cable; pulse amplitude drops from ~0.94 V at 288 K to 0.48 V at 14 K.
fields.figure_caption: Fig. 5: Cryogenic prototype and experimental results. (a) Developed circuit boards. (b) Experimental setup. (c) Simplified circuit configuration. (d) Gaussian-shaped waveform generated at 14 K with a sampling rate of 40 Msps. The dashed curve is a Gaussian fit to guide the eye. (e) Temperature dependence of the Gaussian amplitude (top) and width (bottom), extracted from Gaussian fits to the measured waveforms. Error bars represent one standard error obtained from the fitting covariance matrices. The horizontal axis is broken between 40 K and 288 K.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured voltage versus time showing a 40 Msps Gaussian pulse at 14 K, along with fitted pulse amplitude and width plotted against temperature from 14 K to 288 K.

fields.result: Circuit compilation guided by an operator Schmidt time lower bound reduces QOC critical-path pulse duration by an equally weighted mean of 42.50% across 13 benchmark instances compared to EPOC, yielding a geometric mean speedup of 2.00.
fields.question: How can circuit compilers evaluate the physical control latency of fused unitary target blocks before computationally expensive pulse optimization?
fields.prior: EPOC and PAQOC; EPOC synthesis relies on unitary distance while PAQOC uses average gate latency for width-based block timing estimates.
fields.limits: Evaluated on numerical simulation of a 1D nearest-neighbor chain with fixed coupling limits ($\Omega/(2\pi)=100\,\mathrm{MHz}$, $\bar{g}/(2\pi)=20\,\mathrm{MHz}$), zero drift, zero inter-block coupling, and max block size of 3 qubits.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5. Latency relative to same-instance EPOC. (a) Mean surrogate and QOC reductions. (b) All 104 SCOPE QOC results: circles mark runs, diamonds eight-run means, segments minimum–maximum ranges, and the dashed line EPOC. Vertical offsets separate coincident runs. The left panel compares mean surrogate and QOC reductions for thirteen instances, with larger gains for Heisenberg and HHL. The right panel plots all 104 SCOPE QOC durations relative to the corresponding EPOC result. Every point lies to the left of the baseline ratio of one.
fields.figure_gloss: Surrogate and QOC critical-path latency reductions relative to EPOC across 13 benchmark instances, showing all 104 individual SCOPE runs strictly outperforming baseline EPOC.

fields.result: Short-time Quantum Speed Limits (QSLs) predict Quantum Mpemba Effect orderings at times $t^{\ast} \ll \tau$ prior to trajectory crossings, yielding recall $P \approx 0.8$ and precision enrichment ${\rm PE} \approx 3$ in collective spins and open spin chains.
fields.question: Can features of initial transient dynamics and Quantum Speed Limits anticipate anomalous Quantum Mpemba Effects before a system nears stationarity?
fields.limits: Predictions degrade when late-time trajectory crossings dominate. Analytical short-time expansion $s_{\rm TD}=-K$ assumes non-singular initial velocity $V=\mathcal{L}\rho_0$, requiring full finite-time indicators for pure-state ensembles.
tools: Trace-distance and relative-purity quantum speed limits
Short-time geometric scores ($s_{\rm TD} = -K$, $s_{\rm RP} = B$)
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Diagnostic measures ( $P$ , PE, FDR) vs $t^{\ast}$ for the collective-spin model ( 15 ) with $S=10$ , $\omega_{0}=1$ , $(\kappa_{-},\kappa_{+},\kappa_{z})=(1,0.3,0.5)$ , and $\epsilon=10^{-3}$ , using the TD-based (solid) and RP-based (dashed curves) QSL indicators ( 2 ) and ( 3 ), respectively. The dashed vertical line corresponds to the inverse gap of ${\cal L}$ , the dashed horizontal line indicates ${\rm PE}_{\rm rnd}=1$ . (a) Results averaged over the initial-state class $|\psi_{1}\rangle$ in Eq. ( 16 ). (b) Same as in panel (a) but for the initial-state class $|\psi_{2}\rangle$ in Eq. ( 17 ).
fields.figure_gloss: Recall $P$, precision enrichment ${\rm PE}$, and false discovery rate vs observation time $t^{\ast}$ for a collective-spin model ($S=10$). Short-time indicators reliably predict Mpemba inversions when early trajectory crossings dominate (a), but require times past the inverse Liouvillian gap when late crossings dominate (b).

fields.result: Decomposing full-precision operations into three TF32 products accumulated in full precision accelerates AFQMC walker propagation beyond FP32 and FP64 on Tensor Cores while keeping local-energy deviations well below chemical accuracy ($1\text{\,}\mathrm{m\text{$E$}_{\mathrm{h}}}$).
fields.question: Can mixed-precision arithmetic on GPU Tensor Cores accelerate AFQMC propagation without corrupting accuracy?
fields.prior: Direct single-precision (FP32) propagation achieved substantial speedups with roughly $1\text{\,}\mathrm{m\text{$E$}_{\mathrm{h}}}$ error (Shee et al.).
fields.limits: Evaluated on 1D hydrogen chains up to $\text{H}_{640}$ in STO-3G basis across 200 propagation steps; memory-bound by storing $\Ord{(N_{\text{AO}}^{3})}$ Cholesky matrices on a single GPU.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Left axis, solid lines and markers: Wall time required to propagate 100 walkers along 200 AFQMC steps on the GPU in full, reduced, and mixed precision, plotted on a log-log scale. Right axis, dashed lines and open markers: Speedup relative to double precision. Both are averaged over the five random seeds. Note that we do not optimize the single-precision propagation, so on this GPU it is not much faster than double precision; mixed precision is faster in all systems. For 640 orbitals, propagating both one- and two-body terms in mixed precision is more than twice as fast as double-precision propagation.
fields.figure_gloss: Propagation wall time (left axis) and speedup relative to FP64 (right axis) versus number of atomic orbitals for 100 walkers across 200 AFQMC steps. Mixed precision on Tensor Cores consistently outperforms both FP64 and FP32 baselines, with speedup widening as system size grows.

fields.result: Simulating cylinder wake dynamics via Koopman-von Neumann transport to 1% relative root-mean-square field error requires 1.62 h on about 560,000 physical qubits. Three-coordinate wake runtimes span hours to weeks under one million physical qubits.
fields.question: Can early fault-tolerant quantum computers feasibly simulate nonlinear fluid flows via ensemble transport without prohibitive circuit costs from grid discretization?
fields.limits: Polynomial reduced-order models with fixed dimension and drift degree; assumes surface-code fault tolerance with early fault-tolerant overheads; hardware run relies on reference-circuit noise mitigation.

fields.result: Two-dimensional emergent-coupling-based ansatz (ECBA) achieves $89.38\%\pm 2.26\%$ relative energy accuracy with 5 full on-hardware optimization iterations on a 16-qubit quantum processor, and $97\%$ accuracy on a 49-qubit processor using pre-optimized parameters.
fields.question: Can strong-disorder renormalization group flow guide shallow variational quantum circuits to correct renormalization approximations in two-dimensional disordered quantum systems?
fields.limits: Demonstrated for 16 qubits over 5 hardware iterations and 49 qubits with classical pre-optimization; disconnected gate clusters miss some non-local correlations without parameter depth scaling.
fields.figure_gloss: Plots optimization convergence and hardware layouts along with spatial correlation matrices comparing quantum processor measurements with tensor network baselines for 16-qubit and 49-qubit systems.

fields.result: Timelike block suppression factor reaches $\mu_T = 1.47 \pm 0.25$ from patch sizes $3\times 3$ to $7\times 7$. Walking stability circuit suppresses temporally correlated $|3\rangle$ leakage errors, reaching a logical error floor of $\le 3.20 \times 10^{-8}$ at 60 cycles.
fields.question: How do temporally correlated physical error mechanisms affect logical error suppression across space and time in surface code stability experiments?
fields.limits: Logical error floor at 60 cycles limited by ionizing radiation error bursts. Patch sizes $6\times 6$ and $7\times 7$ restricted to $Z$-basis only due to device layout constraints.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: a) Measured walking (blue) vs. standard non-walking (red) stability logical error on a $3\times 3$ patch of surface code. Walking stability data run a 999-cycle $3\times 3$ $Z$ -basis circuit on a single subgrid for $2\times 10^{7}$ raw shots. Extracting non-overlapping subsampling windows yields $2\times 10^{7}$ effective shots for $c\leq 30$ (one window per shot) and $5.4\times 10^{8}$ ( $1.6\times 10^{8}$ ) effective shots at $c=36$ ( $c=122$ ) from $27$ ( $8$ ) tiled windows per shot, with error bars spanning binomial probabilities within a factor of $1{,}000$ of the maximum likelihood ( ${\sim}3.7\sigma$ , showing upper bounds where zero errors occur). b) Windowed detection fraction for the error burst causing the walking floor. The red region highlights a failed subsample.
fields.figure_gloss: Stability logical error probability versus syndrome extraction cycles on a $3\times 3$ patch. The walking stability circuit bypasses the $|3\rangle$ leakage-induced plateau of the standard circuit, lowering the error floor by two orders of magnitude to $\le 3.20 \times 10^{-8}$.

fields.result: Combines quantum prolate diagonalization with compressed sensing, reducing the sample complexity from $\mathcal{O}(N_{s})$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N_{s})$ sampled points of the autocorrelation function. Resolves molecular Hamiltonian energies to within 1 kcal/mol on trapped-ion hardware using circuits up to 448 two-qubit gates (1221 gates total).
fields.question: Can sparse sampling and matrix completion reduce the quantum execution overhead of quantum prolate diagonalization while retaining chemical accuracy under realistic noise?
fields.prior: Standard quantum prolate diagonalization required $\mathcal{O}(N_{s})$ samples (Stroschein 2026).
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a two-orbital active-space model of an arginine-tryptophan residue pair using first-order Trotterized time evolution; larger systems explored only numerically in the weakly correlated regime.

fields.result: Branch-and-bound solver with see-saw heuristic initialization and greedy row reordering computes exact classical bounds for bipartite Bell matrices up to $130 \times 130$ and $81 \times 321$, improving lower bounds to $K_{\mathrm{G}}(3) \ge 1.438746$, $K_{\mathrm{G}}(4) \ge 1.486092$, $K_{\mathrm{G}}(5) \ge 1.498904$, and $K_{\mathrm{G}}(7) \ge 1.499667$.
fields.question: How can exact classical bounds of two-outcome bipartite full-correlation Bell inequalities with large numbers of settings be computed efficiently?
fields.prior: For $d=3$, best published rigorous lower bound on $K_{\mathrm{G}}(3)$ was $1.43670$ (Designolle et al. 2026). On $60 \times 60$ random matrices, standard branch-and-bound ran in mean $12\,854$ s.
fields.limits: Worst-case search complexity remains exponential. Computational performance degrades if matrix-dependent preprocessing depth is suboptimal; cannot yet solve the $120 \times 120$ $E_8$ matrix instance.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Best mean runtimes over the tested preprocessing depths, $T_{A}^{*}(n)$ , for BB (squares, solid line) and IBB (circles, dashed line). Each mean uses 50 matrices and the shortest of three runs for each matrix and setting. Dotted curves show the reference laws in Eq. ( 17 ), from $n=40$ to the largest tested size for each algorithm. Connecting lines guide the eye; the reference curves describe the measured trend and are not complexity bounds.
fields.figure_gloss: Best mean runtime in seconds versus matrix size $n$ on random square matrices, comparing standard branch-and-bound (BB) to the improved algorithm (IBB).

fields.result: No polynomial-size symmetric quantum circuit family with 1- and 2-qubit gates can compute $\mathscr{P}_{\mathrm{CFI}}^{\mathrm{Alt}}$ if its entanglement width is $o(n/\log n)$. The bound holds even for symmetry restricted to $\mathrm{Alt}_n$.
fields.question: Can symmetry restrictions on quantum circuits be used to establish unconditional circuit lower bounds?
fields.limits: Circuits restricted to 1- and 2-qubit gates, symmetric under input permutations (or alternating group $\mathrm{Alt}_n$), with entanglement width at most $o(n/\log n)$.

fields.result: Proves optimality for Low Autocorrelation Binary Sequences (LABS) of lengths $n=2$ to $30$ using a quantum-classical hybrid branch and bound (QCBB) with fixed-angle QAOA ($p=12$ and $p=1$, $1{,}000$ shots per node).
fields.question: Can a quantum optimization algorithm deliver a certified proof of optimality for the LABS problem rather than merely finding good heuristic solutions?
fields.prior: Classical branch and bound proved optima up to $n=66$ (Packebusch and Mertens 2016), while Gurobi reached $n=41$; prior quantum methods only returned heuristics without bounding gap or certifying optimality.
fields.limits: Proven range limited to $n\leq 30$ in noiseless simulation; runtime node count grows by a factor of roughly $1.9$ per unit $n$ (95% interval $1.59$–$2.37$); claims no quantum speedup.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Convergence of the bounds with QAOA at $p=12$ , QAOA at $p=1$ and SA as the sampler of the same algorithm (settings of Section 4.1 , $1{,}000$ shots per node, one process, seed 1; measured). (a) The blue line is the upper bound, the energy of the incumbent, and the vermilion line the certified lower bound, both as functions of the runtime in seconds, on the instances $n=24,26,28,30$ (rows) for the samplers (columns) QAOA with the fixed angles at $p=12$ and at $p=1$ , and simulated annealing (not run at $n=28,30$ ). A solid black line marks the optimum $E^{*}$ , aligned to $0$ ; between the dashed lines at $\pm w$ the $y$ axis is linear, outside them logarithmic. LABS has no infeasible sequences, so in place of QCBB’s cost of the worst feasible solution we take the half-width $w=E^{*}$ of the linear band, which then holds every bound between the trivial lower bound $0$ and $2E^{*}$ . The ticks inf and $-$ inf mark the time before the first incumbent and before the first certified bound ( $g=1$ there). The PDI of the run, the area between the curves with the gap normalized by $\mathrm{UB}(t)$ ( Section 4.1 ), is written in each panel. At $n=24,26$ the first sampler call, on the master, takes $1.2$ and $5.0$ s at $p=12$ . At $n=28,30$ the master is not sampled ( Section 4.1 ), and the incumbent descends as the nodes below it are sampled. (b) PDI against $n$ for the three series ( $n=2$ – $30$ for QAOA, $2$ – $26$ for SA) and, with broken lines and open symbols, for the two reference series of Section 4.3 at $n=16$ – $30$ (uniform samples, and the optimum supplied at the root with no samples afterwards, whose PDI at $n=18$ , a single node, is below the axis range); vertical lines mark the instances of (a). For $n\geq 27$ the master is not sampled ( Section 4.1 ), so the first incumbent comes from the skew-symmetric restriction (odd $n$ ) or from the first class root (even $n$ ). Every run proves the QOBLIB optimum.
fields.figure_gloss: Upper bound (incumbent energy, blue line) and certified lower bound (vermilion line) plotted against wall-clock time, showing convergence to the certified optimum for $n=2$ through $30$ under QAOA and classical samplers.

fields.result: Observable interference corrections decay as $\exp(-\mathrm{const}\sqrt{d})$ in space-time volume $d$. Simulating time-ordered and out-of-time-ordered correlators in random circuits achieves polynomial run-time scaling in circuit size and target precision.
fields.question: Can classical trajectory-sampling algorithms simulate quantum physical observables in typical random circuits with controlled error and polynomial efficiency despite interference effects?
fields.limits: Demonstrated for 1d brickwork random Haar circuits and 1d $U(1)$-conserving random circuits; ensemble-averaged analyses and small-to-moderate circuit depths.
tools: matrix product state master equation evolution
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: Relative error (squared) $\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}^{2}$ , Eq. ( 26 ), for the addition algorithm combining $R$ horizontal partitions for different $\ell$ at $T=500$ (solid) and extrapolating $T\rightarrow\infty$ (dotted). Results for one (blue), combining two (orange), four (green) or six (red) partitions $Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{6}$ , Fig. 6 . A fit to the four partition data (green, solid) yields the scaling $e^{-0.8\ell^{1.0}}$ , finite size effects are discussed in App. G.4 .
fields.figure_gloss: Squared relative error $\epsilon_{\mathrm{r}}^2$ plotted against spatial partition width $\ell$ at $T=500$ and extrapolated $T\to\infty$. Error decays super-exponentially with partition width as the number of combined partitions $R$ increases from 1 to 6.

fields.result: Two superconducting resonators coupled via DC-biased SQUIDs to a common auxiliary mode of loss $\kappa_b$ exhibit an exceptional point at $\xi_{\mathrm{EP}}=|\delta|/(1+|\delta|)$, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement within $\sim 0.3~\mu$s for private decay rate $\gamma_d/2\pi=0.5$ MHz.
fields.question: Can static flux-tunable SQUID couplings to a single lossy auxiliary resonator realize an exceptional point, transient synchronization, and transient entanglement via engineered shared dissipation in circuit QED?
fields.limits: Small-phase linear regime of SQUIDs, rotating-wave approximation, Markovian limit $\kappa_b/2 \gg \max\{\sqrt{g_1^2+g_2^2}, \gamma_{d,1}/2, \gamma_{d,2}/2, |\Delta_1|, |\Delta_2|\}$, and simulation rather than experimental measurement.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4 : Transient entanglement generated by collective dissipation, obtained from Eq. ( 42 ) (solid lines). (a) Dependence on $\xi=0,0.4,0.6,0.8,0.9$ at fixed $n=0.1$ , with the private decay held fixed. (b) Dependence on $n=0,0.05,0.1,0.2,0.5$ at fixed $\xi=0.8$ . (c) Same as (b) for $3$ dB of initial squeezing. Panels (a) and (b) use $6.5$ dB ( $s=0.75$ ) and panel (c) $3$ dB ( $s=0.35$ ) of squeezing, with identical squeezing orientations and $\Delta_{1}=\Delta_{2}=0$ . Dashed black lines in (a) and (b) show the full three-mode model with $\kappa_{b}=200$ . In (b), the dotted line marks $\tau_{\mathrm{sync}}$ for $\alpha_{1}=1$ , $\alpha_{2}=e^{i5\pi/6}$ , and $\epsilon=0.01$ , and the shaded band marks the coexistence of $R\leq\epsilon$ and $E_{N}>0$ for $n=0.1$ . Displacements affect the synchronization marker but not $E_{N}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Logarithmic negativity $E_N$ plotted against dimensionless time $\tau$ for different cross-decay parameters $\xi$ and thermal occupations $n$, showing transient entanglement generated from initial local squeezing via collective dissipation.

fields.result: Electro-optic quantum transducer using stepped GaAs/AlGaAs quantum-well exciton polaritons achieves predicted transduction efficiency over 60% with under 0.01 added noise quanta across a $\sim$60 MHz bandwidth at pump power below 10 µW.
fields.question: Can quantum-well excitons be engineered via the quantum-confined Stark effect to yield high-efficiency, high-bandwidth, low-noise microwave-to-optical quantum transduction under low pump power?
fields.prior: Vacuum electro-optic coupling is up to five orders of magnitude larger, and pump power is reduced $\sim$6400-fold compared to thin-film lithium niobate devices with equivalent loaded quality factors.
fields.limits: Theoretical design with numerical simulation; assumes low-density bosonic exciton regime; subject to failure modes if discrete exciton states fall within a $4\omega_b$ frequency band around the idler line.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Transduction performance. (a) Illustration of the polariton levels and transduction process as the cavity is detuned through the HH 0 exciton. (b) The pump power $P_{c}$ , (c) peak transduction efficiency $\eta$ , and (d) added noise $n_{\mathrm{add}}$ at the impedance matched ( $\mathcal{C}=1$ ) point as a function of the cavity-exciton detuning $-\Delta$ for different bias fields. The color of the curves corresponds to the character of the polariton with red corresponding to a more cavity-like and blue a more exciton-like polariton. The solid line corresponds to 1 V/µm while dashed/dashed-dotted correspond to 1.5 V/µm and 0.5 V/µm, respectively. The cavity and exciton line widths are fixed at $\kappa/2\pi=12.5$ GHz and $\gamma/2\pi=5$ GHz, respectively, and the calculation includes the higher-order exciton states.
fields.figure_gloss: Pump power $P_c$, peak transduction efficiency $\eta$, and added noise $n_{\mathrm{add}}$ as functions of cavity detuning and polariton composition, showing efficiency $>60\%$ and added noise $<0.01$ at microwatt pump powers.

fields.result: Diagonal energy corrections via Löwdin partitioning substantially suppress spectral errors caused by two-level truncation in ultrastrong coupling, but refitting constant Rabi model parameters leaves systematic deviations for actual circuit parameters.
fields.question: To what extent do truncated higher atomic levels alter low-energy spectra in ultrastrongly coupled multilevel circuits, and where do two-level or perturbative Rabi models remain quantitatively accurate?
fields.limits: Restricted to second-order perturbative treatment of higher atomic levels; full rediagonalization with off-diagonal terms fails to improve accuracy when state mixing becomes non-perturbative.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Comparison of transition spectra calculated using the full multilevel circuit Hamiltonian, the two-level truncated model, and the second-order Löwdin approximations. “Löwdin diagonal” denotes state-specific diagonal energy corrections evaluated using the full $Q$ -space resolvent [Eq. ( 10 )], whereas “Löwdin full” denotes rediagonalization of the symmetrized second-order effective Hamiltonian including off-diagonal matrix elements [Eq. ( 11 )]. (a) Circuit parameters fitted to the experimental spectrum in Fig. 1 (e). (b) Same as (a), but with $\gamma=\alpha$ , corresponding to the absence of the additional shunt capacitance. (c) Same as (a), but with all atom–resonator coupling matrix elements $g_{ij}$ reduced by a factor of eight.
fields.figure_gloss: Transition frequencies plotted against normalized external magnetic flux $f$. The full circuit spectrum is compared to the two-level truncated model, diagonal Löwdin corrections, and rediagonalized second-order effective models.

fields.result: Embedding off-resonant ladder quantum memory in Mach-Zehnder interferometer converts $\sum_n a_n |n\rangle \to \sum_n a_n |n\rangle |n\rangle$ deterministically without optical nonlinearities. Effective number-shift infidelity is $1 - F = n^2 / (4|\alpha|^2)$ under strong coherent control.
fields.question: Can quantum memories mediate photon-photon interactions and deterministic number-correlated entanglement without strong optical nonlinearities?
fields.limits: Requires strong coherent retrieval control field ($|\alpha|^2 \gg n^2$). Doppler dephasing lowers retrieval efficiency; assumes perfect balance to prevent dark-port leakage.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: The Quantum Memory Interferometer (QMI). An input signal photon prepared in the $|{-}\rangle=(|H\rangle-|V\rangle)/\sqrt{2}$ polarisation state is split into two spatial paths by a Polarisation Beam Displacer (PBD), travels through the atoms, and is stored and retrieved by the quantum memory process. Counterpropagating to the signal is a control beam comprising of two pulses separated in time. The control pulses are split into two orthogonal polarisations by a 50:50 beamsplitter and a HWP. In the case when storage and retrieval has occurred in both arms, each of the control pulses will have an extra $n$ photons added. Due to the anti-symmetric nature of the signal and this addition, when these control beams interfere at the second 50:50 beamsplitter, they produce an $n$ -photon Fock state at the dark port of the MZI.
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic of quantum memory interferometer showing input signal split across dual rails, ladder memory storage/retrieval, and dark-port output of number-correlated states.

fields.result: Memory-assisted MDI-QKD protocol via in-memory matter-photon interference halves the required quantum memories and detectors, scaling secret key rate as $O(\sqrt{\eta})$ and surpassing memoryless benchmarks at shorter distances.
fields.question: Can quantum memory-assisted MDI-QKD be simplified and improved by interfering a stored matter qubit directly with a travelling photonic qubit in a single memory?
fields.prior: Two-memory assisted MDI-QKD requires two separate memories and double the detector count, with interference performed on a conventional beamsplitter after retrieving both photons.
fields.limits: Simulations assume symmetric links and asymptotic regimes without finite-size effects. Memory lifetime of telecom-ORCA must exceed several nanoseconds via rephasing or hyperfine control to beat memoryless links.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Comparison of the SKR between the memoryless, two-memory and in-memory protocols for (a) 25% (b) 50% (c) 75% and (d) 100% storage/retrieval efficiencies ( $\eta_{s}=\eta_{r_{0}}$ ).
fields.figure_gloss: Secret key rate plotted against total transmission distance for memoryless, dual-memory, and single in-memory MDI-QKD protocols across memory efficiencies of 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%.

fields.result: Analytically designed six-step CCZ gate protocol operating at finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction $|V|\sim\Omega$ using two Rydberg states with opposite-sign van der Waals shifts ($C_6^{rr}/2\pi=289\text{ GHz}\cdot\mu\text{m}^6$ and $C_6^{rR}/2\pi=-281\text{ GHz}\cdot\mu\text{m}^6$). Total gate time is $t_g=2\pi/\Omega_1+4\sqrt{3}\pi/V+2\pi/V$.
fields.question: How can a native three-qubit CCZ gate be implemented on neutral atoms in optical tweezers when the Rydberg interaction strength is comparable to the driving Rabi frequency rather than in the strong-blockade regime?
fields.prior: Fast Rydberg-antiblockade CCZ protocol (Su et al. 2020), which drops steeply in fidelity as interatomic distance increases.
fields.limits: Numerical master-equation simulation for $^{87}\text{Rb}$; assumes negligible exchange interaction ($|J_6|t_g/l^6\ll 1$); thermal position fluctuations evaluated at $T_a=2\,\mu\text{K}$ with 1000 Monte Carlo samples.
tools: two-level Rydberg excitation with opposite-sign interactions
Monte Carlo sampling of thermal position fluctuations
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: (a) Gate fidelity versus total gate time $t_{g}$ for both proposed paths, evaluated using the TPO and UO measures. The inset shows $t_{g}$ as a function of the interatomic separation $l$ . (b) Comparison with the CCZ gate based on RAB, showing higher fidelities for the proposed paths at larger separations. (c) Gate error $1-\bar{F}$ versus $l$ for both paths, obtained from Monte Carlo simulations incorporating thermally induced fluctuations in the atomic positions. The trapping parameters are $\lambda_{f}=1.064~\mu\mathrm{m}$ , $w_{f0}=1~\mu\mathrm{m}$ , $T_{a}=2~\mu\mathrm{K}$ , and $U_{m}=1~\mathrm{mK}$ , with the trap depth expressed in temperature units. The Rabi frequency is fixed at $\Omega_{1}/2\pi=1~\mathrm{MHz}$ throughout.
fields.figure_gloss: Gate fidelity against total gate time $t_g$, comparison with the Rydberg-antiblockade CCZ protocol across interatomic distances, and gate error ($1-\bar{F}$) under thermal position fluctuations.

fields.result: In a Kitaev-chain quantum reservoir, protected Majorana edge modes yield retention scaling as $\tau_{\rm e}\sim e^{N/\xi}$, balanced by local write-read residue $\mathcal{R}_{\rm loc}\sim\tau_{\rm e}^{-2}$. Interactions ($U\neq 0$) autonomously load bulk memory into edge parities via second-order Liouvillian coupling at the expense of retention.
fields.question: Can a physical system hosting protected topological information perform reservoir computation via its bulk dynamics while retaining processed information in its protected boundary modes?
fields.limits: Numerical reservoir task simulations performed at $N=10$, $\Delta=t$, and $t\tau=1.5$; analytic linear reservoir description strictly requires $U=0$; requires ensemble-averaged readout without mid-circuit back action.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Interaction-induced memory consolidation and edge retention. (a) TSC and Trivial denote the topological superconducting and trivial phases, respectively. The color scale shows the bulk–edge loading $W$ from the center-derived bulk into the edge mode. Loading vanishes at $U=0$ . (b) Mean edge retention $S$ of the edge mode. Interactions enable loading at the cost of edge retention. The open circles in (a,b) mark the topological operating point used in (c–e). (c) Memory function for local and edge-augmented readouts in the topological phase, with a trivial reference using $\mathcal{B}+P_{\rm end}$ . (d) Target and held-out predictions for a temporal integration task with $\tau_{\rm tar}=100$ , using the local features $\mathcal{B}$ and the augmented feature set $\mathcal{B}+P_{\rm end}$ . (e) Test $R^{2}$ as a function of the target memory timescale $\tau_{\rm tar}$ . Parameters are $N=10$ , $\Delta=t$ , and $t\tau=1.5$ , with $\mu/t=1$ and $U/t=0.5$ for the topological phase in (c–e); the trivial reference in (c) uses $\mu/t=3$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Bulk-to-edge loading $W$ and edge retention $S$ across chemical potential $\mu/t$ and interaction $U/t$, accompanied by delayed-input memory function and temporal integration test $R^2$ showing performance gains from including the endpoint parity $P_{\rm end}$ at long timescales $\tau_{\rm tar}$.

fields.result: Local ground-state quenches at atomic array edges or internal interfaces accelerate relaxation to steady state compared to bulk quenches, mediated by boundary-accumulated superradiant modes at early times and suppressed bulk subradiant modes at late times.
fields.question: How do boundary modes, directional dissipation, and internal interfaces influence the quantum Mpemba effect in driven-dissipative waveguide QED?
fields.limits: Weak-excitation regime restricted to collective ground state and single-excitation manifold ($\sum_{\mu=1}^N |p_\mu(t)|^2 \ll 1$). Born-Markov approximation. Resonant driving ($\delta=0$) perpendicular to the waveguide ($\theta=\pi/2$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: QME in a dissimilar atomic array with physical boundaries and an internal interface. (a) Steady-state distributions of two arrays with BE phase are coupled together at $D=0.4$ , with $\xi_{1}/\pi=0.2$ and $\xi_{2}/\pi=0.3$ , respectively. Each subarray consists of $40$ atoms with a total $N=80$ . The inter-array distance between two subarrays is chosen as the average of $\xi_{1}$ and $\xi_{2}$ . (b) Time dynamics of $T$ after quenching certain atoms at specific sites. (c) Late time evolution of $T$ after quenching atoms in (b). Normalized spatial distributions of (d) the most subradiant and (e) the second most subradiant eigenmodes.
fields.figure_gloss: Trace distance $T$ vs time $\gamma t$ and subradiant mode distributions for an $N=80$ two-segment array. A quench at interface site $j=39$ crosses the trajectory of bulk quench $j=20$ around $\gamma t \approx 10$, relaxing faster at late times due to low mode overlap with subradiant bulk modes.

fields.result: Window propagation computes first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits at arbitrary depth in classical polynomial time with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error $\varepsilon=1/\mathrm{poly}(n)$. On 512-qubit Clifford circuits with 768 $T$-gates, mean-squared error drops from $1.97\times 10^{-2}$ to $1.31\times 10^{-4}$ as window width increases from $2\log_2 n$ to $5\log_2 n$.
fields.question: Are out-of-time-order correlators classically hard to simulate?
fields.limits: Applies strictly to first-order OTOCs in 1D; does not apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Accuracy of our window propagation on Clifford-plus- $T$ circuits. (a,b) Comparison of our algorithm with exact simulation for $80$ instances of Clifford-plus- $T$ circuits for $n\in\{256,512\}$ . Black circles indicate exact simulation, and colored symbols show the results of our algorithm for window widths of $w\in\{2\log_{2}n,\,3\log_{2}n,\,4\log_{2}n\}$ and $w=5\log_{2}n$ also shown at $512$ qubits. (c) Mean squared error (MSE) as a function of window width for $n\in\{128,256,512\}$ . The shaded area spans the middle $95\%$ of MSEs obtained at each window width by resampling the circuits with replacement [ 63 ] . At $128$ qubits and $w=4\log_{2}n$ , some resamples miss the only circuit with nonzero error. The lower bound of the confidence interval is zero, though it cannot be represented on the logarithmic axis and is instead indicated by an arrow.
fields.figure_gloss: OTOC values per circuit instance and mean squared error against window width $w$ for 80 Clifford+$T$ circuit instances at $n \in \{128, 256, 512\}$ qubits.

fields.result: Simulated $X$ and $Z$ logic gates achieve $>99.7\%$ fidelity at 1.15 ns gate times in $\text{Fe}^{2+}\text{:forsterite}$ at temperatures up to 10 K. Natural tunnel splitting is $\Delta = 0.19\text{ K}$ (4.040 GHz) under zero field.
fields.question: Can the intrinsic zero-field splitting of a non-Kramers $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ ion in forsterite host coherent qubit operations robust against thermal decoherence up to 10 K?
fields.prior: Prior non-Kramers $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ qubits (Smoleński et al.) required deliberately engineered lattice-mismatch epitaxial strain in CdSe/ZnSe quantum dots to induce degeneracy, demonstrated only spin-state characterization and optical readout, and had no coherent gate-control mechanism.
fields.limits: Theoretical simulation only; spin-phonon coupling constant $G_E$ is unmeasured; Raman and Orbach relaxation rates omitted because prefactors $C_R$ and $A_O$ are unknown; readout methods require lower temperatures than 10 K.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: The strain-drive gate infidelity of the system vs decoherence rate at T = 10 K. The figure shows that at estimated decoherence rate the infidelity of the X and Z Gate logic gates are extremely low.
fields.figure_gloss: Gate infidelity of $X$ and $Z$ gates as a function of decoherence rate at $T = 10\text{ K}$, showing infidelity remains below $10^{-3}$ at predicted direct-process relaxation rates.

fields.result: Collective coupling near half-excitation $k=N/2$ scales nearly linearly with $N$, speeding excitation transfer, but relaxation from the additional excited qubits offsets the gain. Mechanical anharmonicity of $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ raises single-photon target probability from $19.6\%$ to $99.7\%$ for $N=4$ qubits, while pair-dependent qubit-qubit interactions degrade optical retrieval efficiency from $58\%$ to $35\%$.
fields.question: Can a collective superconducting qubit ensemble coupled to a mechanical intermediary overcome weak electromechanical coupling to improve microwave-to-optical quantum transduction?
fields.limits: Theoretical model and master-equation simulations; assumes identical transmons and prescribed heating power-laws from optomechanical crystals.
tools: Master equation simulation with disorder and noise
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Kerr-assisted selective transfer and sensitivity to imperfections. The $N=4$ ensemble starts in $\lvert D_{2}^{4},0_{m},0_{o}\rangle$ . The Kerr-on calculations use the prescribed anharmonicity $\alpha_{m}/(2\pi)=100~\mathrm{kHz}$ , corresponding to $K_{m}/(2\pi)=-50~\mathrm{kHz}$ under $\alpha_{m}=-2K_{m}$ , with the first mechanical transition tuned to resonance. Sequential, nonoverlapping $\sin^{2}$ coupling pulses have peak amplitudes $g_{\mathrm{sm}}/(2\pi)=3.81~\mathrm{kHz}$ and $G_{\mathrm{om}}/(2\pi)=3.43~\mathrm{MHz}$ . (a,b) Lossless mechanical loading without and with a prescribed Kerr nonlinearity. Blue and orange curves show mean ensemble and mechanical occupations, respectively, while purple dotted curves show $P(D_{1}^{4},1_{m},0_{o})$ . (c) Subsequent lossless optical readout with superconducting ensemble–mechanical exchange switched off. Orange/teal curves show mechanical/optical occupations and solid/dashed curves correspond to Kerr-on/Kerr-off loading. (d)–(f) Final target probability $P_{\mathrm{tar}}=P(D_{1}^{4},0_{m},1_{o})$ versus (d) mechanical damping at $\bar{n}_{\mathrm{th}}=0,0.1,1$ , (e) independently varied $T_{1}$ and $T_{\phi}$ , and (f) static frequency-disorder width $\sigma_{\omega}/g_{\mathrm{sm}}$ . The disorder curve and shading give the mean and $10^{th}$ – $90^{th}$ % across realizations.
fields.figure_gloss: State populations over time during transfer from $|D_2^4, 0_m, 0_o\rangle$, showing suppression of multi-phonon leakage and boost in target single-photon probability with $100\,\mathrm{kHz}$ mechanical anharmonicity.

fields.result: Harmless faults in postselected non-Clifford circuits are determined by stabilizer projection on an underlying code defined on the $t$ non-Clifford gates. Cultivation checks using GHZ folds halve fault tolerance to $d = (\delta + 1)/2$ on distance-$\delta$ codes, whereas verified cat checks preserve full distance $d = \delta$, certified up to $\delta = 9$.
fields.question: Which faults are harmful in magic-state cultivation circuits containing real non-Clifford gates, and how can cultivation checks maintain the full code distance?
fields.prior: Clifford S-proxy designs predicted fault distance equal to code distance $\delta$, but real-$T$ simulations showed distance drops to $(\delta+1)/2$ for $\delta=3, 5$.
fields.limits: Deterministic postselected single-qubit target states ($|T\rangle$ or $|\mathrm{CCZ}\rangle$) with no stabilizing Pauli operators besides identity; ideal noiseless final stabilizer decoding stage unless explicit noisy schedule is modeled.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Fault distance with real T gates (filled) and code distance $\delta$ (open), the most that the S proxy can reach. The proxy reaches $\delta$ in every case where we certified it, except the distance-five circuits of Refs. [ 22 , 16 ] , whose proxies have fault distance four. The vermilion gaps are the distance lost to real T gates. (a) GHZ folds, including the circuits of Ref. [ 22 ] , and the surface-code scheme of Ref. [ 16 ] (squares). At $\delta=11$ and $13$ the triangles are the lowest proven upper bounds over the binary folds we evaluated, from Lemma 5 and the fold tree alone, and at $\delta=9$ the lowest of these bounds is certified for a fold without stabilizer rounds (Appendix F.1 ). (b), (c) Cat-state checks without and with verification. At $\delta=9$ the verified cat in (c) is the check without stabilizer rounds, and at $\delta=7$ it keeps the full distance with and without flagged stabilizer rounds around it. (d) Nearest-neighbor cat checks on a square grid. At $\delta=9$ both (c) and (d) are certified by the integer program of Appendix E.6 .
fields.figure_gloss: Real-T fault distance compared to target code distance $\delta$. Unverified GHZ folds achieve only $d=(\delta+1)/2$, while verified cat architectures preserve full distance $d=\delta$ up to $\delta=9$.

fields.result: Any Boolean arithmetic circuit can be implemented with constant quantum depth and constant reaction depth using homogeneous $Z$- and $X$-type Pauli Product Measurements and Toffoli states, at the expense of exponential space overhead and dirty ancilla qubits.
fields.question: How to formalize reaction depth and optimize fault-tolerant Boolean logic circuits under LDPC-native measurement gatesets?
fields.limits: Requires exponential space overhead and leaves intermediate ancilla qubits dirty.

fields.result: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computation requires only a constant number ($\\le 20$) of external control wires on an $n$-qubit chip, executing $n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$ logical qubits with depth-3 periodic geometrically local operations.
fields.question: How much external control is strictly necessary to operate a fault-tolerant universal quantum processor?
fields.limits: Asymptotic analysis. Assumes a noiseless global clock and physical noise on all operations below a universal positive constant. Logical gate time is $n/{\sf polylog}(n/\epsilon)$ without instantaneous classical wires.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 7 : Transformation of a brickwork-connectivity circuit into an upward propagating tile with inputs entering at the bottom and leaving at the top. Circles indicate the locations of qubits physically in a two-dimensional plane. Arrows overlaying the blue circuits indicate the direction of qubit data propagation. Shaded circles are qubit locations where two-qubit gates are applied while unshaded circles contain ancilla qubits required to implement the qubit data propagation using $\mathsf{SWAP}$ . The circuit has period 3: Layers $i\equiv 0\textrm{ mod }3$ apply the indicated gate (or single qubit operations) to each pair of qubits. Layers $i\equiv 1\textrm{ mod }3$ swap shaded locations with their downstream neighbors while layers $i\equiv 2\textrm{ mod }3$ swap shaded locations with their upstream neighbors. The number adjacent to each gate indicates the layer in which it is applied. Adjacent qubits in the 1D line may be swapped without directly interacting by applying the $\mathsf{SWAP}$ in an ‘X’ pattern in round two immediately before the gate location. Importantly, though, at each physical location in the tile where layer-2 gates are applied, whether this X $\mathsf{SWAP}$ occurs or not is fixed, so that the circuit has period 3. This avoids certain correlated weight-2 errors stemming from a $\mathsf{SWAP}$ failure that would otherwise be present. See also [ gottesman2000fault , Section 3] .
fields.figure_gloss: Unrolling of a 1D brickwork quantum circuit into a 2D tile where qubits propagate continuously upward across a physical planar lattice.

fields.result: Two-dimensional color codes reach optimal encoding rates of $1/3$ at distance $3$ and $1/4$ at distance $4$. In a linear ion chain model, simulated $[[20,4,4]]$ and $[[16,4,4]]$ codes hit break-even at two-qubit gate infidelities of $0.22\%$ and $0.26\%$.
fields.question: What are the optimal encoding rates for small, low-distance 2D color codes, and can they achieve break-even performance in trapped-ion chains?
fields.prior: Bivariate bicycle codes with weight-5 stabilizers required $[[30,4,5]]$ and $[[48,4,7]]$ implementations with Shor-style extraction (Wang et al. 2024).
fields.limits: Numerical simulation only. Holds strictly for color codes with only color boundaries on surfaces with Euler characteristic $\chi \geq 0$.
tools: Linear trapped-ion chain circuit-level noise model
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : The break-even two-qubit gate infidelity of distance- $3$ and distance- $4$ two-dimensional color codes. Break-even is defined as the point where the logical error rate equals the physical error rate. Here, the logical error rate is the probability per logical qubit that a logical error occurs during a single quantum error correction cycle. The physical error rate refers to the probability $p$ with which errors are inserted in the ion chain noise model (see Table 1 ). The x-axis shows the total number of qubits used in the quantum error correction cycle. Plots showing the full logical error-rate curves are given in Figure 11 .
fields.figure_gloss: Break-even two-qubit gate infidelity plotted against total qubits required per QEC cycle across distance-3 and distance-4 2D color codes. Shows $[[16,4,4]]$ and $[[20,4,4]]$ breaking even above $2\times 10^{-3}$ physical error rate using 36 to 46 qubits.

fields.result: Using a stationary entangled singlet partner to flag bit flips on a shuttled ancilla restores circuit distance from 1-4 up to 5 or 6 on weight-8 and weight-10 codes, raising the Gross code $[[144,12,12]]$ circuit distance from 7 to 10 in both bases.
fields.question: Can preparing a mobile shuttling ancilla as part of an entangled spin singlet catch propagating hook errors and restore circuit distance in qLDPC syndrome extraction?
fields.prior: CAbLECAR mobile ancillas kept only three-eighths to three-quarters of code distance, falling to circuit distance 1 at check weight 12.
fields.limits: Circuit-level Pauli noise model only, shuttling routing uses heuristic schedules, and exact distances are schedule-dependent.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Distance-6 codes under the uniform model, in which every error source scales with $p$ and transport bit flips occur with probability $p/10$ per hop: BB72 ( $w=6$ ) and the weight-8 and weight-10 codes (instance a). Logical error rate per round over 6 rounds in the $X$ (top) and $Z$ (bottom) basis. Black squares: CAbLECAR; blue diamonds: singlet flag. Open markers, dashed lines: BP+OSD; filled markers, solid lines: exact minimum-weight decoding (Sec. VIII ). Every shot is decoded both ways. Triangles: 95% upper limits where exact decoding recorded no failure. Grey lines: the slopes $p^{2}$ and $p^{3}$ . Error bars: 95% confidence intervals.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate per round versus physical error rate $p$ for distance-6 codes of weights 6, 8, and 10 decoded via BP+OSD and exact integer programming. Exact decoding reveals gains of up to 70x-90x over CAbLECAR that BP+OSD underreports.

fields.result: QuFrame closes the QEC feedback loop within a 1 µs round budget with fallback decoding in 144 ns, cutting the logical error rate by an average of 38.5% compared to a serialized blocking baseline.
fields.question: How can a quantum controller track the Pauli frame in real time with bounded per-instruction latency under multi-core dispatch and decoders of variable latency?
fields.prior: A serialized blocking controller, as modeled in XQsim (Byun et al., 2022), increased logical error rates by up to 4.1× over an ideal zero-latency controller.
fields.limits: Evaluated on a distance-3 rotated surface code with 17 physical qubits; IBM Heron coherence times prolonged 10× in simulations; fallback lookup table memory scales poorly for higher code distances without truncation.
tools: Helios simulator with IBM Heron noise model
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 . Controller overhead impact on logical error rate (LER). We evaluate a rotated surface code ( $d=3$ , 9 rounds, 50,000 shots) on the V80 FPGA, prolonging IBM Heron ( AbuGhanem, 2025 ) coherence times $10\times$ and scaling its noise rates. The ideal baseline assumes no dispatch or decode latency; the blocking baseline serializes frame access and stalls qubits during decoding.
fields.figure_gloss: Logical error rate versus physical error rate scaling factor for a rotated surface code (d=3, 9 rounds). QuFrame avoids stalling and tracks closest to the ideal zero-latency baseline, outperforming the serialized blocking controller across all noise levels.

fields.result: Generalizes pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution to state-dependent operations without approximation. Reaches up to $24\times$ higher throughput than CUDA-Q on distance-3 topological memories with amplitude damping, and up to $83\times$ higher throughput on 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements.
fields.question: Can pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution be extended to circuits with mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels without approximation?
fields.prior: Original PTSBE required stochastic outcomes to be state-independent (mixtures of unitaries), excluding mid-circuit measurements and non-twirled amplitude damping.
fields.limits: Single-precision statevectors; limited by GPU memory for caching intermediate state branches (requires $8\cdot 2^n$ bytes per cached state, e.g., 8 GiB per state at $n=30$ qubits).
tools: generalized pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE)
multinomial branching and cached state reuse
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Speedup of generalized PTSBE over trajectory sampling and near-Clifford simulation. (a) Speedup over trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q (top) and fraction of distinct shots, the number of distinct (trajectory, terminal bitstring) pairs per shot (bottom), against the number of shots $M$ , for three distance-3 memories run for three rounds under amplitude damping. Clifft is not shown, since it can only approximate this noise channel. (b) Speedup at $10^{6}$ shots over CUDA-Q (solid) and over Clifft (dashed), against the density $\eta$ of non-Clifford gates in random monitored circuits of $n=16$ , 24, and 30 qubits and depth $D=8$ . Each Clifford gate is replaced with probability $\eta$ by a non-Clifford Pauli rotation, under the same noise at every $\eta$ . Generalized PTSBE is faster than CUDA-Q at every density and outperforms Clifft beyond a crossover density that falls from 62% at $n=16$ to 24% at $n=30$ . Clifft is faster in the shaded region, where the speedup is below 1. The points labeled AD repeat the $\eta=100\%$ circuits with amplitude damping in place of the Pauli gate noise, which Clifft does not support. Points are geometric means over three runs, and bars show one standard deviation of the log rate.
fields.figure_gloss: Throughput speedup of generalized PTSBE over CUDA-Q and Clifft as a function of non-Clifford gate fraction and total shots across surface codes, color codes, and 16-to-30-qubit random circuits.

fields.result: Families of qubit CSS codes achieve $X$ and $Z$ distances $D_{X}, D_{Z} \ge c_\varepsilon N / (\log N)^2$ and $\mathcal{K} \ge N^{1-\varepsilon}$ encoded qubits per block, supporting $\mathbf{s} \ge N^{1-\varepsilon}$ disjoint matched triples of logical qubits with individually addressable logical CCZ gates selectable via a single transversal physical CCZ layer.
fields.question: Can quantum LDPC codes achieve nearly linear code distance while supporting an almost linear number of individually addressable, transversal non-Clifford logical CCZ gates?
fields.prior: was a single nontrivial transversal logical CCZ gate at distance $N/\mathrm{polylog}(N)$ (Li et al. 2024), or almost linear addressable CCZ yield with polynomial subsystem distance (Golowich et al. 2024)
fields.limits: Contingent on Assumption 1.1 (uniform subfield product expansion of Reed–Solomon codes). Requires initializing all logical qubits outside the $\mathbf{s}$ selected triples to $|0\rangle$.
tools: balanced products of expanding graph covers
uniform subfield product expansion of Reed–Solomon codes
cup products of cellular sheaves on cubes
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Construction of the codes and their logical gates. Complex characters establish expansion, while finite field characters supply the common codewords used to construct cocycles on the balanced product complex. Functionals that vanish on coboundaries make the resulting phase invariant under $X$ stabilizers. Recovering the sheet coefficients and evaluating on an information set makes the pairing diagonal, allowing independent selection of matched logical triples. The distance bound uses Assumption 1.1 . The gate selection uses fixed codes, logical bases, and physical gate locations, with all logical qubits outside the fixed set of matched triples initialized to $\lvert 0\rangle$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Schematic workflow: expanding covers with complex character bounds provide code distance, finite field characters give common classical codewords for cocycles, and dual cycle functionals allow independent selection of transversal CCZ gates via balanced product complexes.

fields.result: Multilayer ion trap with integrated 12.64 GHz spiral resonator drives bare ${}^{171}\text{Yb}^{+}$ hyperfine transitions at $\Omega = 1.2300(27)\text{ MHz}$ with 10 mW input RF. Demonstrates individual addressing of two dressed-state qubits spaced by 10 $\mu$m using amplitude modulation, achieving a dressed Rabi frequency of $3.165(24)\text{ kHz}$ on the target ion while crosstalk excitation on the adjacent ion is unresolvable (expected $\le 0.4\%$).
fields.question: Can an on-chip integrated RF resonator produce an axial magnetic field amplitude gradient sufficient to individually address and manipulate dressed-state trapped-ion qubits without nulling the field at ion positions?
fields.limits: Demonstrated on a two-ion Coulomb crystal; multi-qubit entangling gates not yet implemented; input RF line exhibited 7.4 dB losses before the chip-carrier.
tools: Multilayer microfabricated planar surface ion trap
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Rabi oscillations between the dressed-states of two ions. The ions are prepared in states $\ket{D_-}$ , then an amplitude modulated RF field drives the Rabi oscillations. Finally, the dressed states are transferred into the bare states for the state detection, so dressed state $\ket{D_-}$ corresponds to excitation 0 and dressed state $\ket{D_+}$ corresponds to excitation 1. The RF driving field modulation frequency is adjusted to be equal to $\Omega_{g}$ of the first ion (top). The second ion remains not excited (bottom) as its $\Omega_{g}$ differs by 43 kHz from the modulation frequency. The red curve is a fit with a sine function. Note that the interval from 200 $\mu$ s to 400 $\mu$ s was not measured.
fields.figure_gloss: Excitation probability versus pulse duration for two ${}^{171}\text{Yb}^{+}$ ions separated by 10 $\mu$m driven by a single amplitude-modulated RF field. Top panel shows resonant Rabi oscillations at $3.165(24)\text{ kHz}$ in the addressed ion; bottom panel shows the adjacent spectator ion remaining in its ground dressed state due to a 43 kHz detuning from the axial RF gradient.

fields.result: Trapped odd-parity fermions in multiterminal Josephson networks induce discrete vortex chiralities that suppress $2e$ order and produce algebraically decaying composite $6e$ phase correlations below a BKT temperature $k_B T_{\mathrm{BKT}}^0/J = \pi\sqrt{3}/72 \simeq 0.0756$. In a two-trijunction device, the third harmonic of the free energy dominates below $k_B T_\times/J \approx 0.111$.
fields.question: How can microscopic fermionic parity and spin states in quantum-dot Josephson junctions engineer collective phase order and entanglement in a superconducting network?
fields.limits: Neglects higher harmonics of the odd-parity junction EPR, interdot cotunneling, and self-inductance; classical phase regime assumes island charging energy $E_C \ll J$; weak Gaussian bond disorder treated perturbatively.
tools: exact diagonalization in truncated charge basis
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Threefold Josephson response of two frustrated trijunctions. (a) Odd-parity two-dot device and analog $\pi$ -junction circuit highlighting the phase bias $\delta$ , while the internal phases float. (b) Free energy of the Josephson device as a function of the imposed phase bias $\delta$ at different temperatures. (c) Temperature dependence of the first and third-harmonic responses of the free energy. The dotted line in panel (c) indicates the numerically determined crossover temperature $T_{\times}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Free energy (b) and its first and third Fourier harmonics $A_1, A_3$ (c) as a function of phase bias $\delta$ and temperature $T/J$. Shows the transition from a threefold periodic $6e$ potential to a conventional cosine $2e$ potential crossing at $k_B T_\times/J \approx 0.111$.

fields.result: DIRAC eliminates Nyquist-rate ADCs via analog demodulation and ping-pong integration, using 50.3 pJ per qubit per readout (31.6$\times$ below fixed-point and 238$\times$ below FP32). Total 4 K quantum-classical interface power drops to 0.85 mW per physical qubit, a 50.4% reduction versus fixed-point digital baseband.
fields.question: Can an in-cryostat readout receiver combine frequency-multiplexed qubit readout with neural network discrimination while reducing 4 K power below room-temperature cable loads?
fields.prior: Conventional cryo-CMOS fixed-point digital baseband with 500 MS/s ADCs consumed 1.59 nJ per qubit burst energy (1.71 mW total 4 K power per physical qubit), saving only 36.7% power over room-temperature electronics with flex cables.
fields.limits: Evaluated on 1.12M experimental shots via behavioral models validated against transistor-level simulations over ten mismatch-sampled chips. Requires transmitter/receiver co-design with access to baseband NCO sign bits.
tools: joint matched-filter and neural network training

fields.result: Compiled CAMPS accelerates trajectory sampling by over an order of magnitude compared to uncompiled CAMPS and physical MPS at equal bond dimension $\chi$, while accurately estimating surface-code logical failure rates up to $d=9$ and bivariate bicycle $[[72,12,6]]$ codes under coherent noise at modest bond dimensions.
fields.question: How can one mitigate entanglement growth and large qubit counts to achieve scalable trajectory sampling of quantum error correction circuits under coherent noise using tensor networks?
fields.prior: Uncompiled CAMPS updated Clifford disentanglers dynamically per shot without free-qubit recycling, requiring larger bond dimensions $\chi$ and suffering from order-of-magnitude slower sampling per trajectory.
fields.limits: Demonstrated for rotated surface codes up to distance $d=9$ with coherent $ZZ$ rotations and a $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code with coherent $Y$ rotations under phenomenological depolarizing/coherent noise models, using PyMatching and BP-OSD decoders.
tools: qubit recycling via mid-circuit measurement release

fields.result: End-to-end task-graph orchestration executes circuit cutting, backend dispatch, and quasi-probability reconstruction within a single runtime. Reconstructed observables $\langle Z^{\otimes n}\rangle$ match ideal targets within $0.0562$ across six simulators, with compilation taking $1.11$ to $1.14$ s and reconstruction taking $0.16$ to $0.17$ s.
fields.question: How can the full quantum circuit-cutting pipeline—compilation and cut placement, concurrent backend execution, and post-processing reconstruction—be unified and automated into an end-to-end scheduled task graph?
fields.limits: Wire cutting only (no gate cutting); evaluated mainly on structured, linear GHZ circuits and a MaxCut instance; reconstruction introduces exponential sampling overhead $O(16^{k})$ for $k$ cuts.

fields.result: Direct Pauli evolution via NumPy accelerates two-layer full LiH variational evaluations 3.45-fold over elementary-gate simulation, whereas an RTX PRO 6000 GPU yields roughly 30-fold speedup over an 18-thread Aer CPU baseline for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM in FP64.
fields.question: How should simulation representation, precision, and CPU/GPU resource allocation be jointly chosen to minimize the cost of repeated variational quantum circuit energy evaluations under accuracy and hardware constraints?
fields.limits: Evaluations assume fixed-parameter scalar energy calls, not full optimizer convergence trajectories; unobserved vectors outside candidate comparison subsets are not certified; MPS requires low entanglement.

fields.result: Expanding quantum annealing to width $W=2$ in a random quantum neural network exponentially reduces required depth $L_{min}$ under linear annealing for unstructured search. A tuned quantum perceptron of depth $L=1$ and width $W=2$ solves the search problem with exponentially small error.
fields.question: Can broadening the width of a quantum annealing process through a quantum neural network architecture improve annealing efficiency across quantum phase transitions?
fields.prior: Standard quantum annealing on unstructured search requires minimal depth scaling as $L_{min}\propto 2^N$ with linear schedule, or $L_{min}^{(G)}\propto \sqrt{2^N}$ via Grover schedule.
fields.limits: Complexity scales exponentially with network depth as $W^L$; state reconstruction success probability falls as $1/W^L$ for orthogonal states; tested on small qubit counts or via mean-field factorized product states ($N=400$).
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Minimal depth $L_{min}(\delta)$ of a random quantum annealing network in the quantum search problem. Here $L_{min}(\delta)$ is the minimum depth where the average success probability becomes greater than $1-\delta$ . Here $\delta=1/3$ . Panels (a) and (b) compare the performance of standard quantum annealing (QA) for linear and Grover annealing schedules with that of the quantum neural network for different width $W$ . The weights $w_{ab}^{(l)}$ of neural network are independent random variables uniformly distributed in $(0,1)$ . The phases $\theta_{a}^{(l)}$ are independent random variables from a normal distribution of mean zero and variance $1$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Minimal annealing depth $L_{min}(\delta)$ versus system size $N$ for unstructured search at threshold $\delta=1/3$. Linear schedule depth drops exponentially from $W=1$ to $W=2,3$, while Grover schedule performance is unchanged by width.

fields.result: Two-step adiabatic evolution with non-overlapping clauses prepared as initial $W$ states achieves runtime scaling between roughly $N^{1/3}$ and $N^{1/4}$ for Exact Cover 3, significantly outpacing standard adiabatic Grover scaling.
fields.question: Can adiabatic quantum algorithms achieve faster runtimes than the standard Grover quadratic speed-up when solving NP-complete problems?
fields.prior: Conventional adiabatic algorithms and unstructured Grover search yield runtime scaling of $N^{1/2}$ (Grover 1997; Roland & Cerf 2002).
fields.limits: Neglects environment effects, losses, and decoherence. Assumes unique solution (or very few solutions) near percolation threshold $m \approx 2n/3$, with pairs sharing at most one clause.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Comparison between the conventional scheme ( 1 ) and the step-wise algorithm ( 6 ) proposed here for a specific example. The top panel depicts the considered Exact Cover 3 instance with 21 bits (black horizontal lines) and 14 clauses (green triangles). The $m_{1}=7$ non-overlapping clauses are arranged on the left-hand side and the remaining $m_{2}=7$ clauses to their right. The unique solution $w$ is given in the column on the right-hand side. The middle panel shows the lowest two eigenvalues (black and red curve) of the Hamiltonian ( 1 ) as a function of the interpolation parameter $f(t)$ as well as the probability overlap between the instantaneous ground state $\left|\psi_{0}(t)\right>$ and the initial ground state $\left|s\right>=\left|+\ldots+\right>$ (yellow curve) and the final ground state $\left|w\right>$ (green curve), respectively. In analogy, the bottom panel displays these values for the step-wise algorithm ( 6 ), where the initial ground state $\left|\tilde{s}\right>$ is the reduced superposition state ( 4 ). For the latter, the minimum gap is around a factor of three larger and the Landau-Zener two-mode description ( Adiabatic Evolution ) a much better approximation.
fields.figure_gloss: Lowest two eigenvalues and ground-state overlaps plotted against interpolation parameter $f(t)$ for standard interpolation versus the proposed two-step scheme, showing a minimum gap roughly three times larger for the proposed method on a 21-bit, 14-clause Exact Cover 3 problem.

fields.result: Lean 4-verified QCCD compiler eliminates 11 defects found in prior tools, scaling to 512 qubits in 1 to 29 minutes, and enables co-design where the optimal architecture yields an average 66.4% reduction in execution time over the slowest equal-capacity design.
fields.question: How can quantum charge-coupled device architectures and operating rules be co-designed for specific circuits with verified target code that guarantees correctness and rule adherence?
fields.prior: Unverified compilers (QCCDSim, Muzzle the Shuttle, MQT IonShuttler) contained 11 bugs such as trap overfilling, junction collisions, and illegal middle-of-chain extractions, corrupting hardware comparisons.
fields.limits: Domain analysis rejects programs outside sound bounds; hardware rules cannot inspect arbitrary execution history, classical values, analog pulse shapes, or noise without semantic extensions.

Programs are grouped by circuit interaction graph and ordered by the reduction from the slowest to the fastest design; the mean reduction is 66.4% over all programs and is given per group. The agent’s design is faster than the fastest design on 71 of 75 programs (median reduction 15%), equal on 3 and slower on 1. Bar chart with one column for each of 75 programs, grouped by the interaction graph of the circuit. In each column the slowest equal-capacity design has height one, short ticks mark the other designs, and a filled bar marks the fastest design, whose short name is printed above the column. A narrower bar in a second colour inside each column marks the best design proposed by an AI agent for that program.
fields.figure_gloss: Execution times across 75 quantum programs evaluated on all equal-capacity QCCD architectures, normalized to the slowest design for each program. The fastest design achieves an average 66.4% modeled runtime reduction.

fields.result: Monolithic bilayer $\mathrm{MoSe_2}$-$\mathrm{WSe_2}$ lateral heterojunction achieves photodetection responsivity of 35 A W-1, detectivity of $5 \times 10^{13}\text{ Jones}$, and noise-equivalent power of $6.3 \times 10^{-18}\text{ W Hz}^{-1/2}$, alongside gate-switched spatial electroluminescence and 0.25 kHz CMOS inverter operation.
fields.question: Can a single monolithic 2D lateral heterojunction integrate sensing, light emission, and complementary logic via electrostatic gating?
fields.limits: CMOS inverter operation tested at 0.25 kHz.

fields.result: HgCdTe APDs in linear mode ($M > 400$) achieve external PDE of 42% to 55% with unity-gain QE of 63% (internal PDE 66% to 86%). Intrinsic gain-normalized dark current reaches $I_{\mathrm{dark}}/M = 10.9$ fA at $M = 450$, implying achievable intrinsic DCR of 150 Hz.
fields.question: Can linear-mode HgCdTe APDs achieve single-photon detection with low intrinsic dark count rates required for quantum optics?
fields.limits: Measured at $T = 80$ K. In hybrid RTIA setup, measured DCR is 2.6 MHz to 17 MHz for detection thresholds from 2.5 to 4.5 times amplifier RMS noise; the 150 Hz DCR limit is inferred from CTIA dark current measurements rather than direct single-photon counting.

fields.result: Multivariate trace $\mathrm{Tr}(A_1 A_2 \dots A_k)$ estimated with circuit depth independent of $k$, dominated solely by input state preparation, using $\Theta(k)$ qubits distributable across $\mathcal{O}(k)$ devices.
fields.question: Can multivariate trace estimation be implemented on near-term quantum hardware with circuit depth independent of the number of matrices $k$?
fields.limits: Requires $\Theta(k)$ qubit overhead; depth reduction requires efficient vectorized state preparation oracles for target matrix classes.

fields.result: Sparse-query complexities of guided ground-state energy estimation and preparation scale as $\Theta(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ and $\Theta(\sqrt{s}\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$, respectively, settling the optimal joint parameter dependence.
fields.question: How does the quantum query complexity of guided ground-state energy estimation and ground-state preparation depend jointly on sparsity $s$, overlap $\gamma$, precision $\delta$ or gap $\Delta$, and error probability $\varepsilon$ in the sparse-access model?
fields.prior: Optimal bounds in time-evolution and block-encoding models were $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\delta))$ and $\Theta(\log(1/\varepsilon)/(\gamma\Delta))$ (Jeffery & Witteveen 2026; Jeffery, Somma, Witteveen & de Wolf 2026; Somma & de Wolf 2026), leaving sparsity dependence open.
fields.limits: Lower bounds allow degenerate ground spaces and rely on stoquastic Hamiltonians without geometric locality; upper bounds require reversible in-place sparse-location oracles.

fields.result: t-GQCE maps lattice dynamics to noninteracting quasiparticles on classical CPUs coupled to finite embedding models on QPUs. Adding ghost orbitals suppresses artificial undamped oscillations, yielding double occupancy $0.100$ at $t=5$ for weak quench at $B=7$ compared to DMFT value $0.104$.
fields.question: Can quantum embedding theories be extended to simulate real-time nonequilibrium dynamics of correlated electron lattices on hybrid quantum-classical hardware without continuous bath overheads?
fields.prior: Conventional time-dependent Gutzwiller approximation ($B=1$) produces artificial, undamped coherent oscillations of local observables after an interaction quench.
fields.limits: Embedding states propagated along classically precomputed Hamiltonian trajectories rather than fully self-consistent quantum-in-the-loop evolution; reaches $0.01$ target accuracy only when hardware noise rates are scaled down to one third.
tools: trapped-ion noise models and Quantinuum H2-Emulator
orbital-basis rotation measurements with mirror-circuit mitigation

fields.result: Formulating imaginary time evolution as an environment-induced quantum operation inside FALQON achieves ground-state preparation across arbitrary initial states where standard FALQON stalls, reaching success probability $p=1$ within roughly $1000$ layers on MaxCut.
fields.question: Can dissipation-induced non-unitary dynamics improve the convergence and circuit depth of feedback-based quantum algorithms?
fields.prior: Unitary ITE-FALQON required approximations or ancilla overhead on quantum hardware to apply non-unitary exponential suppression factors; standard FALQON stalled at $r \approx 0.86$ and $p = 0.35$ on average by layer $k=1500$ in MaxCut simulations.
fields.limits: Numerical simulations up to circuit depth $k=1500$; interaction with the environment is modeled phenomenologically without physical reservoir engineering or realistic gate/thermal noise.

(a) $\beta$ , (b) approximation ratio $r$ , (c) probability of success $p$ as functions of the layer $k$ with random initial states $\rho_{0}$ . (d) Number of layers required to prepare a state with $p\geq 0.5$ , with fixed initial state $\rho_{0}=\ket{+}^{\otimes n}\bra{+}^{\otimes n}$ , and random graph weights.
