fields.figure_gloss: Differential conductance $G$ versus gate voltages $V_{\mathrm{G}1}$ and $V_{\mathrm{G}2}$ at $B_\parallel = 0\text{ T}$ and $3\text{ T}$, comparing experiment to attractive two-site Hubbard simulations. Honeycomb charge stability diagrams show paired transitions at $B_\parallel = 0\text{ T}$ and splitting into single-electron regimes above the pairing field.

fields.result: Joint simulated-annealing search over natural-orbital transformations and active-space selections reproduces exact ground-state energies and angular momenta $J$ for $^{19}\text{O}$ and $^{21}\text{O}$ using $|A|=11$ active orbitals instead of the full $sd$ space of $N_{\rm sp}=12$.
fields.question: How can complex many-fermion ab initio problems beyond classical limits be mapped onto compact single-particle bases suitable for classical solvers using low-depth quantum circuits?
fields.limits: Demonstrated only on a valence-neutron shell-model model space with $N_{\rm sp}=12$ under noiseless classical quantum circuit simulation.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: (a, b) The gs energies obtained via different methods and inputs as a function of $|A|$ for 19 O and 21 O. (c, d) The absolute deviations of the gs energies ( $|\Delta E|$ ) and $J$ values ( $|\Delta J|$ ) obtained with the hybrid and classical approaches from their respective exact values for 19 O and 21 O.
fields.figure_gloss: Ground-state energy and absolute error $|Δ E|$ and $|Δ J|$ versus active-space size $|A|$ for $^{19}\text{O}$ and $^{21}\text{O}$, comparing the hybrid quantum-classical search against exact full-space and bare-truncation calculations.

fields.result: Square array of quantum dots coupled via proximitized Andreev dots achieves zero edge-state decay length along crystal axes at $\mu=-2\Delta_{0}$ and $t=\Delta_{0}$, yielding chiral transport in $3\times 3$ and an isolated vortex Majorana zero mode with sub-percent splitting in $5\times 5$ arrays.
fields.question: Can a chiral $p$-wave superconductor with well-separated Majorana modes and chiral edge states be assembled from quantum dots in two dimensions?
fields.limits: Nearest-neighbor tight-binding coupling; requires Zeeman splitting larger than cotunneling and crossed Andreev reflection rates; zero-temperature linear-response calculations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Vortex and edge Majoranas in a $5\times 5$ array. (a) Spectra without and with an additional flux through the central superconducting square. Colors give the boundary weight $P_{\mathrm{edge}}$ of the wave functions, as in Fig. 2 (b). (b) Local conductance $G_{LL}$ of a single tunnel-coupled normal lead ( $t_{c}=0.15\Delta_{0}$ ) connected to the middle of the left edge. (c),(d) Quasiparticle probabilities of the Majorana combinations that minimize (core) and maximize (edge) the boundary weight, represented in (a) by the left and right markers at zero mean energy, respectively. (e) Density cuts along the horizontal and diagonal axes of (c), (d).
fields.figure_gloss: Energy spectra and conductance for a $5\times 5$ quantum-dot array. Panels show the emergence of a near-zero-energy vortex core Majorana mode upon adding flux, distinct from boundary-localized edge states, and its signature in local tunneling conductance.

fields.result: Product distributions of measured bit marginals reproduce approximately $90\%$ of hardware energy reduction in QAOA coverage circuits. Global weighted-covariance retention is approximately $0.50$, while a five-variable block exhibits a hidden local deficit with ratios between $0.12$ and $0.28$.
fields.question: Do variational quantum optimization benchmark observables faithfully represent combinatorial problem coverage, and what do aggregate energy reductions conceal?
fields.limits: Observational execution across three fixed-circuit jobs without estimating gate-level noise mechanisms or processor stationarity. Holds for static geographic coverage; operational vehicle routing and temporal constraints are excluded.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 5: Weighted-covariance profiles of the faithful circuit: (a) historical executions; (b) three fixed-circuit jobs. Points are $C_{\alpha}$ and bars are pointwise conditional 95% percentile intervals from 10,000 joint full-bitstring bootstrap draws per pub; job statistics average the four fixed rounds. Dashed lines show the respective global ratios. The five-variable block carries only $3.7\%$ of the ideal global contribution, yet its block-minus-global contrast is below zero in every context under simultaneous bands for all 30 contrasts (Supplemental Material). Pointwise bar overlap is not the contrast test. Different historical transpilations and settings do not isolate mitigation effects.
fields.figure_gloss: Weighted-covariance ratio profiles across individual problem blocks and globally for QAOA on the 51-qubit faithful benchmark. Shows that the global aggregate sits near 0.50 while the low-weight block exhibits a local deficit between 0.12 and 0.28.

fields.result: Cyclic-2 scheduling combining simultaneous diagonalization with traveling-salesman cell CNOT optimization achieves second-order $O(t^{3}/r^{2})$ Trotter error scaling while preserving first-order sub-unitary count $Lr$. For a dihydrogen molecular Hamiltonian, it reaches target precision at circuit depth ~200 where prior strategies require depth >1000.
fields.question: How can the execution order of sub-Hamiltonians in Trotter decomposition be scheduled to simultaneously reduce both algorithmic error and circuit depth without increasing sub-unitary count?
fields.prior: Simultaneous diagonalization, MaxCommuteTSP, and molecular-specific DepleteGroups (all static first-order orderings requiring depth >1000 for the precision cyclic-2 hits at depth ~200 on dihydrogen).
fields.limits: Classical simulations only; tested on systems up to $n=8$ qubits; fourth-order cyclic-10 shows no benefit over cyclic-2 for $r \leq 20$ Trotter steps; small circuit depth disadvantage observed for 8-qubit Heisenberg model versus standard simultaneous diagonalization.
tools: Cell CNOT optimization via Traveling Salesman Problem heuristics
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Performance comparison for the Dihydrogen molecule
fields.figure_gloss: Error versus circuit depth and Trotter step $r$ for dihydrogen simulation ($t=3$). Shows cyclic-2 surpassing DepleteGroups for $r > 3$ and matching precision at circuit depth ~200 that requires depth >1000 for static baselines.

fields.result: Explicit necessary-and-sufficient construction characterizes the full normal cone $N_{\mathcal{Q}}(\vec{p})$ at every nonlocal extremal quantum behavior $\vec{p}\in\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$. For detection efficiencies $\eta \in [0.75, 0.98]$, constructed Bell tests certify strictly more single-round min-entropy from one Bell score than optimized CHSH tests.
fields.question: Which Bell expressions attain their quantum maximum at an arbitrary given nonlocal extremal behavior in $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$?
fields.prior: Normal cone characterized only at the Tsirelson point (Barizien and Bancal 2021) and along a partially entangled curve (Liu et al. 2024).
fields.limits: Restricted to the bipartite two-input two-output ($\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$) scenario; single-round min-entropy evaluated against general quantum side information under an honest detector-loss model.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Normalized supporting family at the two-bit point $\delta=\pi/6$ , in the plane of Alice’s marginal coefficients $(g_{\alpha_{0}},g_{\alpha_{1}})$ . The four vertices are those of Theorem 3 , and the normalized expression $\mathcal{I}_{\delta}$ sits at the origin in this plane. The dashed rectangle is the region of nonnegative weights; the four local comparisons cut it to the quadrilateral.
fields.figure_gloss: The normalized supporting family at $\delta = \pi/6$ plotted in the plane of Alice's marginal coefficients $(g_{\alpha_0}, g_{\alpha_1})$, showing the quadrilateral slice of Bell expressions maximized by the same extremal behavior.

fields.result: Zero-frequency current noise is lower-bounded by $S \geq \sum_{N} hk_{B}T_{N}[(\partial J/\partial T_{N})^{2}/(\ell_{0}k_{B}^{2}) + (\partial J/\partial\mu_{N} - w_{N}^{Q}J_{N}^{C}/e)^{2}]$, evaluated purely via differential thermoelectric and electrical response coefficients.
fields.question: How can current fluctuations in coherent mesoscopic transport under static or periodic driving be bounded directly by experimentally accessible response coefficients without relying on entropy production or dynamical activity?
fields.limits: Coherent noninteracting transport with noninteracting leads; cannot capture partition-induced off-diagonal noise terms.
tools: Cauchy-Schwarz inequality on inner-product space of scattering matrices
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: TRB in a finite-gap NS junction. The normal terminal is electrically biased by $V$ , while the superconducting terminal, with critical temperature $T_{c}$ and gap $\Delta(T)$ , is grounded. Both terminals are at temperature $T$ . Solid curves show the tightness of the TRB for the charge current, namely the ratio between the two sides of Eq. ( 7 ). The TRB is tight when the transport is dominated by Andreev reflection, namely at low temperatures and subgap biases. Dashed curves show the tightness of the hybrid quantum TUR.
fields.figure_gloss: Tightness of the thermo-electric response bound for charge current plotted as a function of electrical bias $V$ across a finite-gap normal-superconductor junction at fixed temperature $T$.

fields.result: Pulse-tube mechanical vibrations cause angular jitter of the spin quantization axis $\sigma_{\theta} = 5 \times 10^{-4} \pm 1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ degrees at 10 ms delay, producing stochastic Larmor frequency shifts that degrade coherence; noise drops to a 350 nanodegrees floor when aligned to the crystal $c$-axis.
fields.question: How do pulse-tube mechanical vibrations in a cryogen-free dilution refrigerator affect spin frequency noise and coherence in anisotropic Kramers spins?
fields.limits: Measurement sequence repetition time 5 s; angle limited to $|\theta| < 4$ degrees because spin-phonon relaxation time scales as $B_0^2$; 40 cm probe-arm mounting introduces setup-specific mechanical amplification.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Vibration induced Larmor frequency jitter. (a-d) Single shot acquisitions of echo inversion recovery at different angles $\theta$ and temperatures as mentioned in the panels. There are 40 traces in each panel. The echo amplitudes are different across panels due to different loss rates of the resonator $\kappa_{\text{tot}}$ at spin resonances leading to a variable power transferred. (e) Echo magnitude histograms at $\theta=0~\text{deg}$ and $\theta=-3.5~\text{deg}$ at 20mK and a delay of 10ms. The inset shows a schematic of how mechanical vibration shifts the spectral hole (dashed gaussians) w.r.t the detection window (solid gaussian). (f) Echo magnitude variances (measured: symbols, model: line) at the delay of 10 ms for different angles at 20 mK. A 2 $\sigma$ confidence interval was found using bootstrapping [ 29 ] on the 400 shot dataset to set error bars on the calculated variance.
fields.figure_gloss: Measured echo inversion recovery traces and resulting echo magnitude variances as a function of angle $\theta$ and temperature, showing strong fluctuation suppression at $\theta = 0$ degrees and at 60 mK.

fields.result: Adaptive Bayesian thermometry reduces the average number of probe measurements required to hit a prescribed estimation-error threshold by a factor of 2.5 compared with unoptimized protocols.
fields.question: Can Bayesian information-gain optimization guide non-equilibrium spin dynamics of quantum probes to accurately estimate the temperature of an ultracold gas with minimal measurements?
fields.limits: Demonstrated for bath temperatures between 500 nK and 1500 nK. Adaptive sequence recalculation and parameter updates introduce significant experimental laboratory-time overhead relative to a priori optimization.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 6: Error-threshold measurement number. Number of measurements $k_{\mathrm{t}}$ required for the estimation error to fall below the threshold $\epsilon_{\text{t}}$ marked in Fig. 4 (d), versus the estimated bath temperature $T_{\mathrm{TOF}}$ . Each data point corresponds to one estimation-convergence dataset with a reference temperature $T_{\mathrm{TOF}}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Number of measurements required to reach estimation error threshold $\epsilon_{\text{t}}$ versus bath temperature $T_{\text{TOF}}$ for unoptimized, a priori optimized, and greedy adaptive protocols.

fields.result: Training-free topology-divergence estimate matches transpile-all device selection at about $25\times$ lower latency, ranking measured success on IBM hardware at Spearman $\rho=0.95$ and reducing SLA violations from 42–74 jobs down to a few out of 102.
fields.question: Can a cluster scheduler automatically select the optimal QPU backend for a given quantum circuit to meet a target fidelity floor without running full transpilation on every candidate device?
fields.prior: Selecting candidate QPUs by highest average device fidelity or via level-1 transpilation for every candidate device; picking by average fidelity produced 42–74 SLA violations out of 102 jobs.
fields.limits: Fails across vendors when published calibration figures overstate hardware fidelity (e.g., Rigetti Cepheus by 0.47, AQT IBEX Q1 by 0.25). Device-mean rates cannot differentiate near-identical devices or capture broad output distributions (such as QAOA and VQE). Tested on 6 devices across 4 vendors without neutral-atom targets.
tools: topology-divergence estimate with VF2 subgraph embedding
fields.figure_caption: Figure 9: E9 on the three IBM Heron devices (102 jobs), replayed on measured outcomes: SLA violations (left) and false rejections (right) vs. required success $\tau$ . Raw-fidelity and random placement put many jobs below $\tau$ (42–74 and 51–83 of 102); the estimate filter, with or without a conformal margin, removes almost all of those violations.
fields.figure_gloss: SLA violations (left) and false rejections (right) versus requested success probability $\tau$ for 102 jobs replayed on three IBM Heron devices. Filtering with the topology-divergence estimate keeps violations near zero, whereas raw-fidelity and random placement miss $\tau$ for 42 to 83 jobs.

fields.result: Supersmoothing qDRIFT achieves diamond-norm error $\left\lVert\Phi-\mathcal{U}_{T}\right\rVert_{\diamond}\leq\frac{C}{L}\left(c_{0}^{2}N^{4}T+c_{0}^{4}N^{8}T^{2}\right)$ for many-body Coulomb dynamics. Convergence is first-order in step size uniformly over all $L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3N})$ initial states without domain, smoothness, or energy restrictions.
fields.question: How can continuum many-body Coulomb dynamics be simulated efficiently on a quantum computer despite singular interactions and an unbounded Hamiltonian?
fields.prior: Standard Trotter and conventional qDRIFT exhibit order reduction to $t^{5/4}$ or slower local rates on hydrogen-like states, decaying as slowly as $1/\log L$ for general $L^{2}$ initial states and bounded by $L^{-3/4}$ for $H^{2}$ initial states under conventional qDRIFT.
fields.limits: First-order in time. Asymptotic end-to-end gate bound $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{2}N^{7}/\epsilon)$ assumes charged particles with mass ratios bounded away from zero.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 4: Trace-norm error at $T=1$ for the two-body hydrogen atom initialized in its internal ground state with a Gaussian center-of-mass wavepacket. The dashed lines show $L^{-1}$ and $L^{-3/4}$ for reference.
fields.figure_gloss: Full two-body trace-norm error versus number of time steps $L$ at $T=1$ for hydrogen ground-state dynamics. Lie-Trotter, Strang, 4th-order Suzuki, and conventional qDRIFT stagnate near $L^{-3/4}$ scaling, while supersmoothing qDRIFT surpasses $L^{-1}$ scaling.

fields.result: Canonical polyadic decomposition of real-space grid Coulomb potentials achieves $\mathcal{O}(N^{1/3})$ T-gate scaling per Coulomb term with rank 8, yielding hydrogen atom energies to $\sim 10^{-5}$ Hartree precision at grid spacing $\Delta x=0.6$ Bohr.
fields.question: Can real-space Coulomb potentials in first-quantized grid representations be efficiently decomposed to reduce block-encoding circuit complexity and T-gate scaling on quantum computers?
fields.prior: Tensor hypercontraction and quadrature-based CP representations had required ranks of 15 to roughly 50 to represent Coulomb interactions.
fields.limits: Numerical tests limited to single hydrogen, helium, LiH, and a 1D single-particle pseudo-Coulomb model; neglects two-body Toeplitz optimisations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 8: T-gate count for a single application of a one-body Coulomb term using CP decomposition for different values of $N^{1/3}$ , demonstrating $\mathcal{O}(N^{1/3})$ scaling.
fields.figure_gloss: T-gate count plotted against grid dimension $N^{1/3}$ for a single application of the decomposed one-body Coulomb operator, verifying the $\mathcal{O}(N^{1/3})$ scaling.

fields.result: Discretized Riemannian gradient flow compiled into quantum circuits optimizes models directly within the quantum domain without classical feedback or measurements, decreasing training loss exponentially with iterations for sufficiently small step sizes and bounding generalization error by $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{(d_{\rm eff}^{2}\log(d_{\rm eff} N) + \log(1/\delta))/N})$.
fields.question: Can classical optimizers and intermediate quantum-to-classical measurements be completely eliminated from quantum machine learning training loops?
fields.limits: Circuit depth grows exponentially in training iterations with dataset size as the base of the exponent. Autonomous execution requires loss functions where gradient updates avoid evaluating intermediate expectations.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 3: Performance of unitary learning (a) The training (solid) and testing (dashed) loss functions using $N=20$ training samples are plotted against the number of training iterations. (b) The testing loss after $k=20$ training iterations is plotted against the number of training samples $N$ . (c) The commutator norm $\|[\sum_{i}Z_{i},U_{k}]\|_{2}$ between the symmetry generator and the trained unitary are plotted against the number of training iterations for verifying that the algorithm is aware of the problem’s symmetry from the training data (Theorem 4 ). In all panels, the label “Symmetric sector” and “Full Haar random” refer to the training dataset uniformly drawn from the invariant subspace of the excitation number equal to $1$ and the whole Hilbert space, respectively.
fields.figure_gloss: Training loss, testing loss, and infidelity plotted against iterations (with $N=20$) and sample size $N$ for learning an $n=8$ qubit unitary, demonstrating rapid convergence and symmetry inheritance with few training states.

fields.result: Adding a single-parameter all-to-all contractive layer $\hat{U}_{\text{CT}}=\exp(i\alpha\prod_i\hat{Z}_i)$ between brick-wall layers matches the observable-learning test loss of pure brick-wall circuits with depth $L+1$ at depth $L$ for $L \geq 2$.
fields.question: Can contractive unitary layers enhance the expressivity and parameter efficiency of multi-instance quantum neural networks?
fields.limits: Classical numerical simulations; 5-qubit architecture; idealized state preparation and gate operations without physical noise models.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 2: Numerical results for the observable learning task. (a) Distribution of the target values $y(\psi)$ in the training set. (b) Training and test loss as a function of training epochs, with the number of instances fixed at $R=8$ . (c-d) Test loss after training as a function of the number of instances and the number of trainable parameters, respectively. Different curves correspond to architectures with or without contractive layers and $L\in\{1,2,3,4\}$ .
fields.figure_gloss: Test loss on observable learning versus instance count (c) and trainable parameter count (d) across depths $L \in \{1,2,3,4\}$, showing lower loss and data collapse for architectures with contractive layers compared to standard brick-wall circuits.

fields.result: A pure-gauge $D_{3}$ non-Abelian ladder exhibits Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) spectral statistics and eigenstate thermalization hypothesis behavior, with the GOE parameter region expanding as system size increases from $N=3$ to $N=5$. No quantum scar states appear.
fields.question: How do non-Abelian lattice gauge theories thermalize far from equilibrium when formulated with discrete gauge groups?
fields.limits: Numerical simulations restricted to ladder geometries up to $N=5$ plaquettes, pure gauge Kogut–Susskind Hamiltonian, discrete dihedral group $D_{3}$, and two-dimensional irreducible representation $\mathbf{2}$.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1 : Overview of the spectral-statistics phase diagram. Panel (a) shows the heatmap of the average minimal gap ratio, $\braket{r}$ , in the parameter space spanned by the coupling $\mathrm{g}$ and the plaquette deformation $\varepsilon$ , for $N=5$ . The shaded regions indicate where the system displays GOE-like spectral statistics within the chosen tolerance $(\pm 4\%)$ , after interpolation and smoothing for visualization, with darker shades corresponding to larger system sizes. Their growth with the system size $N$ suggests that the chaotic regime becomes progressively more robust. Panels (b) and (c) show two representative points for $N=5$ : one with accidental Poisson-like level statistics and one in the chaotic regime with GOE statistics. The spectrum is restricted to the even sector of the vertical-inversion symmetry.
fields.figure_gloss: Heatmap and shaded regions of the average minimal gap ratio $\braket{r}$ plotted across coupling $\mathrm{g}$ and plaquette deformation $\varepsilon$, showing the expansion of GOE-like chaotic regimes with system size $N$.

fields.result: Truncation cutoff for pure $U(1)$ gauge evolution error $\leq\epsilon$ scales as $\Lambda_{\mathrm{c}}\leq C_d[g^{-1}\sqrt{F+a\mathcal{E}}+F+a\mathcal{E}]$ for general $d$, improving to $\Lambda_G\leq C_G g^{-1}\sqrt{F+a\mathcal{E}}$ in $d=2$, where $F=\mathcal{O}(\log(a^{-1}g^{-1}T\epsilon^{-1}))$.
fields.question: How to bound the digitization truncation error and required electric field cutoff for Kogut–Susskind $U(1)$ lattice gauge simulation in low-energy subspaces?
fields.prior: Scaled linearly in $T/(ag^2)$ (Tong et al. 2022); required asymptotic cutoff $\sqrt{8}/g^2$ at small $g$ for $d=3$ (Carey et al. 2024).
fields.limits: Pure $U(1)$ lattice gauge theory without matter or background charges on hypercubic lattices; initial states restricted to excitation window $\mathcal{E}$ above the vacuum.
fields.figure_caption: Figure 1: Incidence matrices for two adjacent plaquettes. Solid arrows give the link orientations; dashed arrows traverse both plaquette boundaries counterclockwise. Each row of $C$ sums link angles around one plaquette. The shared link $\ell_{2}$ contributes $+1$ to row $p_{1}$ and $-1$ to row $p_{2}$ (orange); links absent from a boundary contribute zero. Each column of $D$ has $-1$ at the link’s tail and $+1$ at its head, illustrated in blue for $\ell_{2}$ . Thus $D^{\mathsf{T}}$ takes vertex-angle differences along links. Each oriented plaquette boundary has zero net incidence at every vertex, giving $D_{\mathrm{loc}}C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathsf{T}}=0_{6\times 2}$ and, for the full lattice, $DC^{\mathsf{T}}=0$ .

fields.result: Disordered QEC threshold is set by average entropy $\overline{H}[P] = H_c$ (with $H_c = 1/2$ for self-dual surface codes) under optimal maximum-likelihood decoding, while sub-threshold failure decay rate is bounded by the average Bhattacharyya coefficient $\overline{B}[P]$. Under mischaracterization, performance is dictated by average cross entropy $\overline{H}[\Pi]$ and tilted Bhattacharyya coefficient $\overline{B}[\Pi]$.
fields.question: To what extent can accurate characterization of disordered noise processes improve QEC thresholds and sub-threshold scaling, and which functionals govern performance under incomplete knowledge?
fields.limits: Replica fixed-point conjecture assumes Nishimori line arguments extend to disordered duality; deep sub-threshold bounds require large distance $d$ and asymptotic regime $\overline{B}[P] \ll 1$.
fields.figure_gloss: (b) Key information-theoretic functionals governing threshold and decay rate under characterized, uncharacterized, and mischaracterized noise. (c, d) Surface code logical failure rate collapsing at $\overline{H}[P] \approx 0.5$ and decay rate bounded by $\overline{B}[P]$.
